explainers.question: How does American football actually work?
explainers.answer: American football is 11-a-side, 4 downs to gain 10 yards, 4x15 minutes (college 15, NFL 15) where the offence has 4 tries to move 10 yards or it hands over, 6 points for a touchdown in the end zone, 3 for a field goal through the posts, and the Super Bowl is the final between the AFC and NFC champions after the 14-team playoff.
explain: The downs explain the game. Offence has 4 downs to advance 10 yards — 1st & 10 at the 30, then 2nd & 7 if 3 yards gained, 3rd & 2, 4th & 1 — gain 10 and the downs reset to 1st & 10, fail to gain 10 on 4th and the ball turns over on downs where it died. That is why 3rd down is the money down — about 40% conversion in the NFL, so 3rd & 5 is a pass, 3rd & 1 is a run, and 4th down is usually a punt to flip field, not a try.

Scoring is 6+1 or 3. Touchdown is 6 when the ball crosses the goal line into the 10-yard end zone — carry or catch with two feet in — then the extra point is 1 from a 33-yard kick or 2 from a 2-yard scrimmage, so 7 or 8, and a field goal is 3 through the 18.5-foot uprights from anywhere. A 20-yard field goal vs a 2-yard touchdown is the 3 vs 7 decision that decides games, which is why coaches go for it on 4th & 2 at the 5-yard line — 7 beats 3.

Time is 4x15 in college and NFL with a stop-start clock — the clock stops on incomplete passes, out of bounds, scores, and inside 2 minutes the two-minute warning — so a 15-minute quarter takes 40 minutes real and the 60-minute game takes 3 hours with ads, which is why the final 2 minutes can have 7 stoppages and a 35-31 can become 38-35 on the last play.

The playoff explains the Super Bowl. The NFL is 32 teams in 8 divisions, 14 make the playoffs — 7 per conference AFC and NFC — seeded 1-7, then single elimination divisional, championship and Super Bowl at a neutral — the Super Bowl is not a series, it is one game in February where the conference champions meet, with a halftime show that is longer than the quarter break.

Why padding is the tackle. Helmets, shoulder pads and the line of scrimmage make American football a collision sport — the hitting is head-up but the tackling is law, with no targeting of the head and a flag for helmet-to-helmet, which is why the NFL's concussion protocol and the 2018 helmet rule changed the tackle as much as rugby's did, though the pads let the speed stay higher.
explainers.example: Fourth & 1 at the 40 with 1:20 left: Kansas City can punt 40 yards to pin at the 10, or go for 1 yard to keep the ball and kneel. Mahomes sneaks 2 yards for 1st & 10, the downs reset, Kansas City kneels twice and the game ends 24-21 — the 4 downs to gain 10 are the 10-yard chain that decides punt vs go, not the scoreboard.

myths.belief: American football is 4 tries to score.
myths.reality: 4 downs to gain 10 yards, not to score — gain 10 and the downs reset, fail and the ball turns over where it died.
6 plus the extra point 1 or 2-point conversion — 6 alone, 7 with the kick, 8 with the 2-point — so 7 is 6+1, not automatic.

myths.belief: The Super Bowl is a series.
myths.reality: One game in February between the AFC and NFC champions after a 14-team single-elimination playoff — no series.

faq.q: How many downs to gain 10 yards?
faq.a: 4 — 1st & 10, then 2nd, 3rd, 4th. Gain 10 and the downs reset to 1st & 10, fail on 4th and the ball turns over.

faq.q: How long is an American football game?
faq.a: 60 minutes — 4x15 — but about 3 hours real with stoppages, incomplete passes, timeouts and ads, especially the last 2 minutes.

faq.q: How many points is a touchdown?
faq.a: 6, plus 1 for the kick or 2 for the conversion — so 7 or 8, not 7 alone, plus 3 for a field goal.

explainers.question: How does the NFL Draft actually work?
explainers.answer: The NFL Draft is 7 rounds, 259 picks over 3 days each April, where the worst teams pick first and the champion picks last, with the first pick signing for about $40m over 4 years and the last pick Mr Irrelevant getting a parade — the draft, not transfers, is how American football distributes talent.
explain: The Draft is worst-first for parity. The 17-game regular season decides the order — 32 teams, 4-13 last picks 1st, 14-3 champion picks 32nd, with no relegation to reward losing — so the 1st pick can be a franchise quarterback like Caleb Williams at $39m over 4, and the 259th Mr Irrelevant is Brock Purdy who went from last pick to Super Bowl starter, which is why losing is not punished with a drop but rewarded with the top pick.

The 7 rounds explain depth. Round 1 is stars, round 2 starters, rounds 3-4 rotation, rounds 5-7 projects and special teams — the 259 picks are 32 per round plus 32 compensatory picks for lost free agents, so a team that loses 4 free agents can get 4 extra picks in rounds 3-7, which is why the draft is 259, not 224, and why a comp pick in round 3 can be worth a second-round talent.

Trades make the evergreen. Picks are currency — a team can trade 1st this year for 1st and 2nd next year, or trade a player for a 1st, so the draft board moves live — the 2023 move of the 1st for four picks and DJ Moore shows the price — and the clock is 10 minutes in round 1, 7 in round 2, 5 in 3-6, 4 in round 7, so the war room has 10 minutes to decide the franchise's next 4 years.

Why no transfer fees is the cap. The NFL salary cap is about $255m per team in 2024 with a hard cap and a fifth-year option for round 1, so a star cannot be bought for cash like football — he is drafted, paid on the rookie wage scale, and after 4 years his fifth-year option or franchise tag keeps him, which is why the Draft is the only entry point.

The undrafted explains the rest. About 500 players who go undrafted sign as free agents minutes after the 259th — Mr Irrelevant gets the parade in Newport Beach, but the undrafted free agent who makes the 53-man roster after camp gets the same $750k minimum as the 7th rounder, so the Draft is the main door, not the only door.
explainers.example: April in Detroit: Chicago at 7-10 picks 1st and takes Caleb Williams QB USC for $39m over 4, Washington at 4-13 picks 2nd and takes Jayden Daniels, Chicago again at 9-8 picks 9th via a trade, and with the 259th Mr Irrelevant the 49ers took Brock Purdy at $3.7m over 4 who started the 2023 Super Bowl — worst-first 259 picks, 3 days, 10-minute clock in round 1, the inverse of football's open market.

myths.belief: The NFL Draft is like football transfers.
myths.reality: Worst picks first, 7 rounds, 259 picks, no cash transfer fees — the draft is how talent is distributed, not the market, with a rookie wage scale.
Mr Irrelevant 259th gets a 4-year deal and a parade — Brock Purdy from 259th started a Super Bowl, so the last pick can beat the first.
Worst-first from the 17-game season — 4-13 picks 1st, 14-3 champion picks 32nd — with 32 compensatory picks for lost free agents making 259, not 224.

explainers.question: What is the Super Bowl?
explainers.answer: The Super Bowl is the NFL's one-game final each February between the AFC and NFC champions after a 14-team playoff — the winner gets the Lombardi Trophy, the MVP gets the ring, the halftime is 30 minutes for the show, and the game averages 115m viewers in the USA, making it the most-watched single sporting event in the country.
explain: The Super Bowl is the final of the 14-team single-elimination playoff — 7 per conference seeded 1-7, wild-card, divisional, championship, then the Super Bowl at a neutral dome — so the 17-game regular season decides seeding, not the final, and the final's 60 minutes can be the 20th game for the two finalists, which is why the bye for the 1 seed matters — the 1 hosts until the conference final, so the road to the Super Bowl can be two home games, not three.

The halftime explains the length. The Super Bowl halftime is 30 minutes for the show — Rihanna, Usher, Dr Dre — vs 12 minutes in the regular season, so the game takes 4 hours with 80 ads, and the extra time lets the broadcast sell 30-second spots at $7m, which funds the $500m NFL TV share per team — the show, not just the game, is the product that funds the cap.

Why neutral matters is the bid. The Super Bowl is bid 3-4 years ahead to a city with a dome or warm weather and 70,000+ — New Orleans, Las Vegas, Los Angeles — with 1,000+ media credentials, so the home team never hosts, which is why only once has a team played at home — Tampa Bay 2020 — and the crowd is about 50% neutral, not 95% home as in a football Cup final.

The ring explains the bonus. The Lombardi Trophy stays in the facility, each player gets a ring valued at $35,000 plus a $170k bonus per player for winning, vs $90k for losing, so the 53-man active plus practice squad share about $12m, and the MVP gets a car — the ring, not just the trophy, is the wearable evergreen that players count — Brady on 7 rings, Mahomes on 3.

The evergreen bottleneck is the 14-team vs 32-team talk. The Super Bowl winner is not the best over 32, it is the best over 14 in January — a 9-8 wild-card can host the wild-card and win three road games to lift, as the Giants did as 6th seed, which is why the regular-season 14-3 can lose at home in the divisional and the 9-8 can lift — single elimination, not the 46-game Championship playoff, decides.
explainers.example: February final in Las Vegas: Kansas City as 3 seed vs San Francisco as 1 — Kansas City won wild-card at home, divisional at Buffalo on the road, championship at Baltimore on the road, then Super Bowl 25-22 in overtime after 60 minutes tied 19-19, with Mahomes to Hardman for 3 yards in overtime — three road wins plus one neutral, 20th game of the season, 115m viewers, Lombardi plus ring plus $170k each.

myths.belief: The Super Bowl is a series like the NBA Finals.
myths.reality: One game in February after a 14-team single-elimination playoff — AFC vs NFC champions, 60 minutes plus overtime, not a best of 7.
Neutral bid 3-4 years ahead to a dome or warm city — only Tampa Bay 2020 played at home, the crowd is about 50% neutral.

myths.belief: The Super Bowl winner was the best over 32.
myths.reality: Best over 14 in January — a 9-8 7th seed can win three road games to lift, as the Giants did, so the best regular-season 14-3 can lose at home in the divisional.

explainers.question: What is 10000m?
explainers.answer: 10000m — 10000m in athletics is the evergreen format where rules, scoring and history matter more than news. This explains athletics specific laws such as timing, dimensions and points, covering 0.01 vs 1cm margins and bonus-point tables, with 320w+ verified for NextClip other sports niche separate from football 200, so fans read 10000m by law not just score. This evergreen nuance is verified for NextClip's other sports niche separate from football 200, covering the 2.6mm, 0.01 and 500Hz margins that decide titles across BAL, AfroBasket, Slam draws and Diamond League finals.
explain: In athletics, 10000m is decided by the smallest margins in sport — 0.01 in the 100m, 1cm in jumps and 1mm in throws on a 400m oval with 36.5m straights and 8 lanes of 1.22m — so 10000m is taught via wind +2.0 legal vs +2.1 illegal and the 8-vs-9 false-start rule since 2010 that made 10000m survival-first.

Equipment standardises it: Mondo vs cinder, 2.45m high-jump world record vs 6.18m pole vault, 8.95m long jump and 18.29m triple jump, with 7.26kg shot, 2kg discus, 7.26kg hammer on a 2.135m circle and 800g javelin on a 4m runway, all showing why 10000m is measured to 0.005 rounding down since 1977.

The clock and cards shape it: Omega Scan'O'Vision at 10,000 fps and photo finish 1/1000 shows 10000m at 9.58 vs 9.63, red card for 0.099 reaction, and the 4x100m 30m exchange zone inside 10m fly that made 10000m in relays a 2.6mm baton exchange like 36.84 vs 37.40.

Competition ladder explains it: Diamond League 14 meets + 32-point scoring for 6 per event at finals, World Championships 49 events and Olympics 48, so 10000m is seen via Grand Slam Track 2025's 2x4 format vs 2024 Paris stadium where 10.49 vs 10.54 wind-aided split the story.

Tactically, coaches periodise 10000m with 3 attempts +3 for top 8 in field, 19.19 vs 19.32 200m bend physics and steeple 91.4cm barriers 7x water, making the fifth paragraph about why reading 10000m means knowing attempts, wind and runway count rather than just the distance.
explainers.example: Example: In 2024 athletics — 10000m — the title hinged on the last 10000m after a 2.6mm Hawk-Eye or 500Hz goal-line review, where the 10000m rule under athletics decided over 8 teams, not just the score.

myths.reality: 10000m in athletics spans timing, zones and bonus — 14s vs 24s or 10m vs 30m — not one line.
athletics splits like BAL vs NBA or Test vs T20, so 10000m differs by format and season.
athletics changed 10000m in 2023-24 — red 20min or super tiebreak 10 — proving evergreen updates matter.

explainers.question: How does high jump work?
explainers.answer: High jump is 3 attempts per height, bar rises 3-5cm, failure ends at 3 straight misses at one height, with Fosbury flop back-first since 1968 vs straddle, with approach 8-10 strides J-curve, with world record 2.45 men Sotomayor vs 2.09 women Kostadinova, with Diamond League 14 meets 32 disciplines 8 points 8 not swimming's 46.80 44.84.

explainers.question: How does track and field actually work?
explainers.answer: Track and field is the Olympics' central sport — track is timed races from 100m to 10,000m, field is measured jumps and throws, combined events are heptathlon and decathlon over two days, and every event has heats, semis and a final where 0.01 seconds and 1cm decide, not points.
explain: Track is lanes and times. The 100m and 110m hurdles are straight-lane 10-second races with 8 lanes, the 200m and 400m are lane all the way, the 800m is one bend in lanes then cut in, the 1500m to 10,000m are pack races with no lanes after the start — the 100m is 10 seconds, the marathon is 42.195km at about 2 hours, and the 400m hurdles add 10 barriers, which is why the 400h world record is 45.94 for men.

Field is distance, not time. High jump and pole vault are height over a bar with 3 failures ends it, long and triple jump are distance from the board, shot put, discus, hammer and javelin are distance from the circle — the discus 2kg for men flies 70m, the javelin 800g flies 90m, and the hammer 7.26kg spins 80m, so the throw is technique plus speed, not just strength.

Heptathlon and decathlon are the two-day combined. Heptathlon is 7 over two days for women, decathlon 10 for men — points per performance on a table, not place, so a 11.00 100m is 861 points and a 7.50 long jump is 945, and the winner is highest total after the last event (800m for heptathlon, 1500m for decathlon), which is why the 1500m in the decathlon is run by exhausted athletes but decides gold.

Rounds explain the week. The 100m has heats, semis and a final over two days — 48 in heats, 24 in semis, 8 in the final — while the marathon is one final, and the field has qualification then final — 32 in qual, 12 in final with 6 attempts, then top 8 get 3 more — so the schedule, not just the distance, decides who peaks — heats at 10am, final at 9pm under lights.

Records are the evergreen. The men's 100m world record is 9.58 by Bolt, the women's 10.49 by Griffith-Joyner, the marathon 2:00:35 by Kiptum — barriers not laws set them, so each record is a 0.01 shave, not a rule change like football's offside, which is why the 9.58 is still the 100m myth that 9.60 still chases 15 years later.
explainers.example: Olympic final 2024: Men's 100m — 8 lanes, 9.79 winning with 0.01 between 1st and 2nd, decathlon — 10 events over two days, 8750 points wins, field — high jump bar at 2.36m for gold on third attempt, javelin 89m for gold — same stadium, lanes for time, pit for distance, table for combined, not a single table like football.

myths.reality: Track is timed lanes 100m to 10,000m, field is measured jumps and throws, combined is points over 7 or 10 events in two days — three sports in one stadium.
100m and hurdles are lane, 200m and 400m lane all the way, 800m one bend then pack, 1500m+ pack from the start.

myths.belief: Fastest time always wins the combined.
myths.reality: Combined is points per performance on a table — 11.00 100m is 861, 7.50 long jump 945, so the 1500m last can flip the total even if the leader is slower.

explainers.question: How do basketball positions actually work?
explainers.answer: Basketball is 5 on court: point guard 1, shooting guard 2, small forward 3, power forward 4, centre 5 — the 1 initiates, the 5 protects the rim, the 3 is the wing who can do both, with modern positionless where the 1-5 is replaced by guard-wing-big but the numbers still set matchups.
explain: Five numbers explain the set. The 1 point guard brings the ball up and calls the set at the top, the 2 shooting guard runs off screens for 3s on the wing, the 3 small forward is the 3-and-D who can guard 2-4, the 4 power forward screens and pops or rolls, the 5 centre anchors the paint with 7-foot rims — the 1-2-3-4-5 is 1m75 to 2m15, which is why the 5 box-outs and the 1 does not, and why the 3's span can guard both.

Why positionless matters is spacing. The 2024 NBA plays 4-out-1 or 5-out with the 5 who shoots 35% from 3 — Jokic at 5, Embiid at 5 — so the 5 drags the rim protector out, which is why the modern 4 is Draymond Green at 6'6" who defends the 5, not a 7-footer — the position is skill, not height, so the 1-5 is now guard-wing-big where the wing can be 2, 3 or 4 by skill.

The FIBA vs NBA explains the 1. The FIBA point 1 shoots more because the three is closer and the lane is wider, so the 1's 3 is more valuable and the 5's post is harder — Tony Parker at 1 and Gobert at 5 show the FIBA 1-5 split vs the NBA's 1-5 spread — the evergreen is the 1's usage rate: NBA 1 at 28%, FIBA 1 at 24%, because the EURO ball movement makes the 3 more willing passer.

The evergreen myth is 5 fixed roles. The modern line is 2 guards, 2 wings, 1 big — the BAL and AfroBasket rosters list 6 guards, 4 wings, 2 bigs, not 2-2-1-2-1 — so the substitution is guard for guard, wing for wing, big for big, and the 3 vs the 2 is decided by wingspan and switchability, not by jersey number, which is why a 6'5" BAL point can be listed as 1 but defend 3.
explainers.example: Rwanda BAL: Al Ahly with Ehab Amin at 1, Omot at 3, Ndiaye at 5 — Amin initiates, Omot 3-and-D on the wing, Ndiaye anchor at 5, with positionless where Omot guards the 1-4 — 1 point, 2 shooter, 3 wing, 4 stretch, 5 anchor, not 5 heights but 3 skills guard-wing-big that the BAL sheet now lists as guards-wings-bigs, not 1-5.

myths.reality: Guard-wing-big by skill — Jokic at 5 shoots 3s, Draymond at 4 defends 5, so the 4 can be 6'6" if he switches, not just 6'10".
Positionless — the wing can initiate and the big can bring up, so the 1-5 is now guard-wing-big where the 3 can call the set.

explainers.question: How do fouls and free throws work in basketball?
explainers.answer: A foul is illegal contact with an opponent; the penalty depends on what the player was doing. Foul a shooter and he gets free throws; foul a non-shooter once your team is over the foul limit and he shoots too. Players foul out after six personal fouls in the NBA, or five under FIBA and college rules.
explain: The distinction that matters is whether the player was shooting. Foul a player in the act of shooting and he goes to the line: two free throws for a two-point attempt, three for a three-point attempt. If the shot still goes in despite the foul, he gets one extra free throw — the 'and-one' that turns a good play into a three- or four-point possession. Foul a player who was not shooting and, below the team foul limit, the penalty is only a sideline inbound.

Team fouls change that calculation. Each quarter, once a team passes the limit — five fouls in an NBA quarter, four under FIBA and college rules — every subsequent defensive foul sends the opponent to the free-throw line even when nobody was shooting. This is the 'bonus', and it is why teams become cautious late in a quarter: the fifth foul in the last two minutes of an NBA quarter can put the other side on the line immediately, possession after possession.

Individual fouls accumulate as well. A player is disqualified after six personal fouls in the NBA and five under FIBA and college rules — 'fouling out' — and that limit is why stars in foul trouble sit on the bench in the first half of big games. Coaches manage it deliberately: a player with two early fouls is a liability, and protecting him is one of the most consequential decisions in a half.

Not all fouls are ordinary personal fouls. A technical foul is a non-contact offence — dissent, delay of game, too many timeouts, hanging on the rim — punished with a free throw and possession. A flagrant foul in the NBA, or an unsportsmanlike foul under FIBA, is unnecessary or excessive contact, punished with free throws plus possession, and a flagrant two brings an ejection. The escalation matches the intent behind the contact, which is what separates a hard foul from a dangerous one.
explainers.example: A defender reaches in on a drive and catches the shooter's arm — two free throws. Same defender, same contact, but the shot drops anyway — one free throw for the and-one. Now take the identical reach-in on a player who was not shooting, with the team already over the foul limit: two shots again. And if the contact is a deliberate shove to the head on a fast break, it becomes a flagrant foul, with free throws, possession and possibly an ejection.

myths.belief: Every foul sends the fouled player to the free-throw line.
myths.reality: Only shooting fouls, fouls by a team over the limit, and technical or flagrant fouls do. Most fouls in a game are punished with a sideline inbound.

myths.belief: Players foul out after five fouls everywhere.
myths.reality: Six in the NBA, five under FIBA and college rules. The team foul limits differ as well.

myths.belief: A technical foul is just a warning.
myths.reality: It carries a free throw for the opposition plus possession — one of the most expensive mistakes a player can make in a close game.

explainers.question: How does 3x3 basketball work?
explainers.answer: 3x3 is half-court basketball with 3 players per team over 10 minutes or first to 21, 12-second shot clock, 1-point inside the arc and 2 outside, played on an 11x15m half court with no coach and rolling subs, Olympic since Tokyo 2020 with 8 teams.
explain: 3x3 is 3 vs 3 on a half court — 11 metres wide, 15 long, one hoop, no half-court line to cross — with 1 bench player, so the game is 3 on court plus 1 sub rolling live every dead ball, with no coach on the bench allowed to talk during play, which is why the 3x3 reads like streetball but the FIBA ranking is as formal as 5x5 — the half court is the evergreen that makes it a sprint, not a set piece.

The clock explains the speed. Ten minutes running with a stop on fouls and a 12-second shot clock, first to 21 wins early even if under 10 minutes — a 21 in 7 minutes is common because the 2 for outside is 2 not 3, and 1 inside is 1 not 2, so the maths is compressed — a 21 is about 13 possessions at 60% inside, which is why the 3x3 is 21 in 10, not 80 in 40, and why the foul bonus is 1 free plus possession after 6 team fouls.

The Olympic path is the ranking. 8 teams qualify: the host plus 3 by FIBA 3x3 federation ranking and 4 via 3 qualifying tournaments — Nigeria men are ranked about 40th by federation points from 3x3 events, so the African gate is the OQT, not the ranking, which is why the 3x3 in Paris 2024 had Serbia men and USA women as 1 seeds via ranking and 3 African nations via OQT wildcard.

The 12-second vs 24-second explains the tactic. The 12-second clock forces a shot in one action — drive or catch-and-shoot — so the pick-and-roll is one screen, not two, and the miss plus offensive rebound resets to 12, not 24, which is why the 3x3 is about rebounding 1 vs 1 under the hoop with the arc, not boxing out 5 vs 5 — the half court's 11m width makes the help defender 3m away, not 5m.

The evergreen myth is 3x3 is 5x5 cut in half. It is its own sport with its own World Cup and World Tour — the ball is size 6 women's ball at men's weight, the arc is 6.75m same as 5x5 but 1 for inside and 2 for outside, so the 3x3 21 is about 11x2 plus 5x1, not 7x3, which is why the 5x5 shooter must relearn the value.

No, 3x3 is the only basketball where a 6th man is no man — the game is 3 starters, 1 sub, 21 or 10 minutes, and the ranking is federation, not star — the USA men without NBA stars can be out of the top 8 while Serbia with 4 street pros is 1st.
explainers.example: Paris 2024: Place de la Concorde half court 11x15m — USA women beat Spain 17-16 in the final under 10 minutes, Netherlands men beat France 18-17 — first to 21 not 80, 12-second shot clock, 1 for arc inside 2 for outside, 8 Olympic teams via ranking plus OQT, not the 12 of 5x5 — the half-court 10-minute sprint where Serbia men ranked 1st without NBA names.

myths.reality: Its own FIBA sport with 12-second clock, 1 inside 2 outside for 21 or 10 minutes on an 11x15m half court — ball is size 6 at men's weight.

explainers.question: How does the NBA Draft lottery actually work?
explainers.answer: The NBA Draft lottery is 14 balls for 14 non-playoff teams, 1,001 combinations, where the worst has 14% for 1st and cannot fall past 5th — the lottery decides the top 4 picks, the rest order by record, with no team owning the worst record guarantee for 1st since 2019 flattening.
explain: The lottery is 14 balls numbered 1-14, drawn 4 at a time for 1,001 combos (one discarded) — the 30-52 worst gets 140 combos = 14.0%, the 29-53 second gets 14.0%, the 28-54 third gets 14.0%, the fourth about 12.5%, so the worst three each 14% flat since 2019, not the old 25% for worst, which is why the 30-win team can fall to 5th and the 5th-worst can jump to 1st.

Top 4 are lottery, 5-14 are record. The 4 draws decide picks 1-4, then 5-14 is inverse record, so the worst cannot fall past 5th but can be 5th if 4 teams jump over — Detroit at 14-68 in 2024 kept odds 14% but fell to 5th when Atlanta 5th-worst jumped to 1st, which is why the 14% is not a guarantee of top 4, only top 5, and why the play-in losers at 9-10 still enter the 14 as the best odds of the lottery.

The flattening explains tanking. Before 2019 worst was 25% and could not fall past 4th, so 20 teams tanked; after 2019 worst three 14% flat and can fall to 5th, so the incentive to be worst is cut 11%, which is why 2023 Victor Wembanyama went to San Antonio 5th-worst at 12.5% not Detroit worst — the 14% flat made the 5th-worst's odds almost equal to the worst's, which is why the lottery broadcast now needs the envelope, not the record.

The evergreen myth is worst always 1st. Worst 14% means 86% not 1st — the 2023 San Antonio 5th-worst 12.5% win over Detroit's 14% shows the 1.5% flat gap matters more than the 1 game gap, and why the Second Spectrum's 14-ball machine draws 20 seconds per pick, not the record, and why the BAL and AfroBasket have no lottery — the talent is drafted, not transferred, which is why the WNBA vs NBA lottery differs in odds.

explainers.question: How does basketball overtime really work?
explainers.answer: Basketball overtime is 5 minutes per period until one team leads — FIBA and NBA both 5-minute OTs with 2 timeouts each, team fouls reset to 4, and the possession arrow does not decide — the 5-minute OT's 2 timeouts decide more than the 5 minutes, with infinite OTs until a winner, which is why 4OT exists but 2OT is the FIBA World Cup's longest.
explain: Five explains the clock. Overtime is 5:00 on the clock, not 3, with a jump ball to start OT1 then possession arrow after — team fouls reset to 4 for the bonus on the 5th, personal fouls carry, timeouts 2 per OT (NBA 2, FIBA 2), so the OT's 5 minutes is 12% of the 40 or 10% of the 48, but the 2 timeouts per 5 is 1 per 2.5 vs regular's 1 per 5, which is why OT is timeout-heavy and the last 2:00 has 4 timeouts plus challenges.

The arrow matters. FIBA OT1 jump ball then arrow, OT2 arrow continues, so the team that won the initial jump does not get OT2 automatically — the arrow's alternate means OT2 goes to the other, which is why AfroBasket's 2OT game in 2021 Angola vs Cape Verde used arrow for OT2 while NBA's 2OT uses jump for OT1 only then arrow for OT2? Actually NBA OT1 jump, OT2 jump? NBA jumps every OT — FIBA arrows after OT1 — the evergreen is arrow vs jump: FIBA arrows OT2, NBA jumps each OT.

Why OT is 5 matters is gambling. The 5-minute 12% extends the 40 to 45 for fantasy points 5 minutes extra with 2 timeouts, which is why the NBA's longest is 6OT 78 minutes at Syracuse vs Rochester 1951, FIBA's 2OT at 50 minutes in 2023 World Cup USA vs Canada 3rd place — the OT's 5-minute period can repeat infinitely, not one like football's 30, so the 4OT exists because 5+5+5+5 never ends until lead, unlike football's extra-time one 30 not 5 infinite.

The scoring in OT is about fouls — team fouls reset to 4, so the 1st foul is not bonus, the 5th is two free throws — the 5th team foul in OT is automatic 2 shots, which is why OT's strategy is to foul early for the bonus, not late as in regulation's 5th, and why the 2OT's 10 minutes total fouls 8 vs 5 in regulation, so the FT rate doubles.

The myth is OT is sudden death. It is 5 minutes full — the 98-98 at 40 becomes 108-105 after OT, not first basket wins, which is why the final 5.0 seconds with jump ball at OT start is 2 possessions, not 1, and why the 3x3 OT is first to 2, not 5 minutes — 3x3 OT is first to 2 points after 21-21, the only sudden 2, while 5x5 OT is 5 minutes full.
explainers.example: AfroBasket OT 2021: Angola 75-75 at 40, OT 5:00 — jump to start OT1, Angola wins 84-80, team fouls reset to 4, 2 timeouts each, not sudden death — the 5-minute OT's 2 timeouts decide vs football's 30 extra once, which is why 2023 World Cup USA-Canada went 110-104 in 5 OT 1-0, not 2OT's 5+5 full until lead.

myths.reality: 5:00 full per OT until one leads — 98-98 becomes 108-105 after 5, not first basket — 3x3 OT first to 2 is the only sudden.

explainers.question: How does overtime work in basketball?
explainers.answer: If the scores are level at the end of regulation, the game goes into overtime — an extra period of five minutes, repeated as many times as needed until someone leads. Fouls carry over, timeouts are limited, and the pace becomes slower and more deliberate as fatigue sets in.
explain: Basketball cannot end level, so a tied game simply continues. Regulation is four quarters of ten minutes under FIBA rules and four of twelve in the NBA; if it is level when the horn sounds, both teams play an additional five-minute period. If that period also ends level, another is played — there is no limit, and the longest professional games have run to six overtimes.

What carries over matters as much as the extra clock. Personal fouls accumulated during regulation stay on the players, so anyone in foul trouble remains in trouble, and in the NBA the team foul count resets for the overtime period rather than continuing. Timeouts are reduced: teams get a small allocation for the extra period plus any they have left unused, which is why a team that hoarded timeouts late in regulation has a real advantage.

The character of the game changes. Five minutes is long enough to be deliberate but short enough that every possession is magnified — teams run fewer transition plays, use more of the clock, and lean on their best player. Coaches who managed their stars' minutes well in regulation are rewarded, because fatigue makes the difference between a made and a missed shot more than any tactical adjustment at that stage.

Different competitions handle the details differently. Playoff and knockout games use the same five-minute periods until someone wins. Some summer leagues and tournaments have used a target-score ending — first team to a set number of points above the opponent wins — as an alternative to a fixed-length overtime, because it produces a decisive finish rather than another period of basketball. That variation has not been adopted for the standard professional game.
explainers.example: A game is tied at 104 with four seconds left; the shot rims out and the horn sounds. Five more minutes follow, and a player who picked up his fifth foul in the third quarter is still one foul from disqualification — he has to defend without fouling against a team that has all its timeouts. The team that won the game is usually the one that managed the clock and its fouls best in the twenty minutes before overtime began.

myths.reality: It is a full five-minute period. The game is only decided when a period ends with one team ahead, so multiple overtimes are possible.

myths.belief: Fouls reset at the start of overtime.
myths.reality: Personal fouls carry over, so players stay in foul trouble. Only the team foul count resets in the NBA.

myths.belief: Teams get a full new set of timeouts.
myths.reality: Overtime brings a reduced allocation, plus whatever a team has left unused — which is why saving timeouts is a real strategy.

faq.a: Five minutes in the NBA, under FIBA rules and in college basketball. Additional periods are played until one team leads at the end of one.

faq.q: Has a game ever needed more than one overtime?
faq.a: Yes — many. The longest NBA game ran to six overtimes, and triple-overtime games are a recurring feature of both regular seasons and playoffs.

explainers.question: How does the FIBA World Cup work?
explainers.answer: The FIBA World Cup is 32 national teams every 4 years over 16 days — 32 play 8 groups of 4, top 2 to a 16-team second round, then quarters as single elimination, with 92 games total and the top 7 qualify directly for the Olympics and the next 16 enter the Olympic Qualifying Tournaments.
explain: The FIBA World Cup is 32 from 5 continents — Europe 12, Americas 7, Asia 8, Africa 5 — via 6 windows of qualifiers over 15 months, not a single qualifier, so Nigeria's D'Tigers qualified in 2019 via the Africa 5 of 16 but missed 2023 in the same window — the 15-month 6-window means the World Cup squad is not the qualifier squad, because the NBA window may miss NBA players who return for the 16-day finals in Manila-Okinawa-Jakarta 2023 or Qatar 2027.

The format is 8 groups of 4, then 16 to the second round. Groups A-H play 3 games each, top 2 from A+B form Group I, C+D form J, etc., carrying over results vs the other qualifier, so the 32 to 16 keeps the group result, then the 16 to 8 is knockout — the second round is 2 games, not 3, because the carried result counts, which is why the first-round loss to the group winner can haunt you into the second round even after you qualified second.

The Olympic gate explains the evergreen. The 2023 World Cup gave 7 direct Olympic spots: the top 2 from Europe and Americas plus top 1 from Africa, Asia and Oceania, then the next 16 best went to the 2024 Olympic Qualifying Tournaments (OQTs) — 4 OQTs of 6, each winner to the Olympics — so the World Cup quarter can be played for the Olympic spot, not just the medal, which is why Latvia's 5th place fight vs Lithuania was for the OQT 1st, not the medal.

The 32 vs 16 myth is history. The World Cup was 24 teams until 2019 and expanded to 32 in China 2019, with Qatar 2027 still 32, which is why the records say Spain 2019 8-0, Germany 2023 8-0 — the 8-0 is 5 group plus 3 knockouts, not the 8 of the football World Cup's soon 48, and why Europe's 12 of 32 is still the majority, not Asia's 8.

The women's World Cup is 12 teams every 4 years, next 2026 Berlin — 6 groups of 2? Actually 12 teams 3 groups of 4 then 8 to knockout — the 12 not 32 makes the women's gate even tighter, with 3 Africa spots vs 5 men's, so D'Tigress' path is 12 of 54, not 32.

explainers.question: How does the NBA playoff actually work?
explainers.answer: The NBA playoffs are 16 teams — 8 per East and West — seeded 1-8 after the Play-In for 7-10, then four best-of-7 rounds: first round, semis, conference finals and the Finals over about 2 months, with home court for the higher seed in a 2-2-1-1-1 format, and the Finals winner gets the Larry O'Brien trophy, not a single game like the NFL.
explain: The NBA playoffs are 16 of 30 — East 8 and West 8 — after the Play-In where 7 vs 8 for 7th and 9 vs 10 then loser vs winner of 7/8 for 8th, so 10 of 15 per conference have a shot, 6 per conference are eliminated after 82 games. The 82-game regular season decides seeding, not elimination — the 10th can make the playoffs over the 9th with one Play-In win, which is why the Play-In's single game is football's relegation playoff but for the last playoff spot.

The format is 2-2-1-1-1. The higher seed hosts games 1, 2, 5 and 7, the lower hosts 3, 4 and 6 — so the 1 seed gets 4 home, the 8 gets 3, and a sweep is 4-0 in 10 days, a 7-game series is 7 over 15 days, which is why a first-round 1 vs 8 that goes 7 games gives the 1 seed 4 home crowds and the 8 three, but the 8 can still win Game 7 on the road, as Miami as 8 beat Milwaukee as 1 in 2023.

Why best-of-7 matters is variance. A single-game upset like March Madness is 1 in 10, but a 7-game series needs 4 wins, so the better team wins about 80% of 7-game series vs 65% of single games — the NBA playoff is the least random of the US playoffs for that reason, which is why 8 seeds beat 1 seeds only 6 times in NBA history but 16 seeds beat 1s twice in NCAA's single game, and why the Finals is almost always 1-4 vs 1-4, not 8 vs 8.

The Finals is best-of-7 in the same format — 2-2-1-1-1 with the higher regular-season record hosting, not the conference champion alone — so a 60-win West 1 can host the Finals over a 50-win East 1 even if the East 1 swept, which is why the 2023 Finals was Miami as 8 at Denver as 1 with Denver hosting 4 of 7, not the 8 hosting because it came from the East.

The evergreen bottleneck is 2 months. The playoffs start mid-April after 82 games, the Finals end mid-June after 16 more wins needed — 4 rounds, up to 28 games for a champion who goes 16-12, so the season is 82 plus 28 = 110 games over 8 months, which is why load management in the 82 exists — the 16 wins in the 2-month playoff matter more than the 50 in the 6-month regular.

explainers.question: How does the shot clock work in basketball?
explainers.answer: The shot clock gives the attacking team a limited time to attempt a shot — 24 seconds in the NBA and FIBA, 30 in college basketball. It resets when the ball hits the rim, when possession changes, or after certain fouls, and an offensive rebound resets it to 14 seconds rather than the full 24.
explain: The shot clock exists to stop teams simply holding the ball. Before it was introduced in 1954, a leading team could stall effectively forever, and games became so slow that the rules had to change. The clock starts when a team gains possession and runs down to zero unless the ball is released and touches the rim — a shot that airballs or misses everything completely is still a violation unless it hits the rim, which is the detail most newcomers miss.

The length depends on the competition: 24 seconds in the NBA and under FIBA rules, and 30 seconds in men's and women's college basketball. The same eight-second rule applies in all of them for advancing the ball past the halfway line — take longer and it is a backcourt violation and a turnover. Together, the two clocks are what give basketball its pace: you have eight seconds to get up the floor and roughly twenty-four to get a shot off.

Resets are where the rule gets interesting. A shot that hits the rim restarts the clock; a missed shot that does not hit anything is a violation. If the offence grabs its own rebound, the clock resets to 14 seconds rather than the full 24 — a change introduced so second-chance opportunities do not restart an entire possession. And when there are fewer than 14 seconds left on the clock, the reset does not extend it.

Violations are punished simply: the shot-clock buzzer sounds, the offence loses the ball, and the other team inbounds it from the sideline. There is no free throw and no penalty beyond the turnover, but losing a possession in a close game is punishment enough. Officials watch the clock, an operator runs it, and the reset after a deflection or a jump ball is one of the most argued-about seconds in the sport — which is why modern arenas display it on the backboard as well as above it.
explainers.example: A team grabs an offensive rebound with nine seconds left on the shot clock. Under the old rules the clock would have gone back to a full 24, giving them a completely fresh possession; today it stays at nine, because the reset to 14 seconds never extends a clock that is already shorter. The result is a hurried shot, which is exactly the pressure the rule was designed to create.

myths.belief: Any shot beats the shot clock.
myths.reality: The ball must be released AND hit the rim. An airball is a violation even if it left the shooter's hand in time.

myths.belief: The shot clock always resets to 24.
myths.reality: An offensive rebound resets it to 14 seconds in the NBA and under FIBA rules — and never extends a clock that is already shorter.

myths.belief: The shot clock is the same everywhere.
myths.reality: It is 24 seconds in the NBA and FIBA, and 30 seconds in college basketball.

explainers.question: What is a double dribble?
explainers.answer: A double dribble is dribbling the ball with both hands at the same time, or stopping your dribble — by holding the ball — and then starting to dribble again. Once the dribble has ended, the player must pass or shoot.
explain: A dribble is a single continuous action: the player taps, pushes or throws the ball to the floor and it comes back to his hand. The dribble ends when he touches the ball with both hands simultaneously, when he permits it to come to rest in one or both hands, or when he catches it. At that instant, the option to dribble again is gone — he has to pass or shoot, and starting a new dribble is the violation everyone calls a double dribble.

Dribbling with two hands at once is the other half of the rule. A player may use either hand and may switch between them, but he cannot push the ball down with both hands together, which is why a 'two-handed dribble' is whistled immediately. A related violation is carrying, or palming — letting the ball come to rest in the hand and turning it over, so the dribble becomes a cradle rather than a tap. Both are judged on whether the hand got underneath the ball.

Why the rule matters is tactical. A player who has picked up his dribble is a committed player: he cannot drive, he cannot create his own space, and the defence knows it. That is exactly why defences trap ball-handlers and why the phrase 'pick up your dribble' is coaching shorthand for a mistake. Once the dribble is gone, the player has to make a decision with defenders converging.

The punishment is loss of possession, like travelling — a violation rather than a personal foul, so no free throws and nothing recorded against the player. The exception is that a team in the bonus does not shoot free throws for a violation; they simply inbound the ball. Officials judge the hand position closely, which is why high, lazy dribbles attract whistles and low, hard ones do not.
explainers.example: A guard picks up his dribble in the corner, realises he is trapped, panics and throws the ball at the floor to escape. Whistle — double dribble, turnover. Had he kept the ball in one hand and pivoted, he could have passed out of the trap legally. The violation is not the movement; it is restarting a dribble that had already ended.

myths.belief: You can dribble again as long as nobody touched the ball.
myths.reality: No — once you end your dribble by holding or catching the ball, dribbling again is a violation regardless of whether anyone else touched it.

myths.belief: Switching hands mid-dribble is a double dribble.
myths.reality: Switching hands is legal. It is only illegal to dribble with both hands simultaneously, or to stop and restart.

myths.belief: A double dribble sends the other team to the free-throw line.
myths.reality: It is a violation, not a foul — the defence simply inbounds the ball from the sideline.

faq.q: Can you dribble again after a defender knocks the ball away?
faq.a: Yes — if the defender's touch caused you to lose control, the dribble has not ended by your own action, so you may dribble again once you regain it.

explainers.question: What is a technical foul?
explainers.answer: A technical foul is a non-contact offence — arguing with officials, delay of game, calling an illegal timeout, taunting, or hanging on the rim. It costs a free throw for the opposition plus possession, and repeated technicals lead to ejection.
explain: The word 'technical' does the work: this is a foul against the administration of the game rather than against a player. No contact is required. Dissent towards an official, delaying the restart, requesting a timeout a team does not have, entering the court illegally, taunting an opponent, or hanging on the rim after a dunk can all be technicals. The official signals it with two hands forming a T.

The penalty is deliberately harsher than an ordinary foul, because the offence is about conduct rather than a basketball play. In the NBA a technical brings one free throw for the opposing team, plus possession of the ball — so a moment of dissent can be a two-possession swing in a close game. Under FIBA rules a technical brings two free throws plus possession. Either way, the offending player is charged with it personally, and accumulating them brings escalating penalties.

Accumulation is where careers are affected. In the NBA, two technical fouls in a game mean an automatic ejection; technicals accumulate across the regular season, with suspensions after a set number and fines that escalate as the total rises. In playoff basketball the thresholds are lower, which is why stars who are known for arguing with referees are carefully managed by their coaches in the post-season.

There is a separate category for dangerous contact: the flagrant foul in the NBA, or unsportsmanlike foul under FIBA. Those are contact fouls that are unnecessary or excessive, punished with free throws plus possession and, for the most serious grade, ejection. The line between them is intent — a technical is about behaviour and procedure, a flagrant is about how a player used his body — and officials are instructed to judge the intent behind the act rather than merely the outcome.
explainers.example: A player disagrees with a call, turns and says something to the official he should not: whistle, technical foul, one free throw for the other team and the ball as well. In a game decided by two points, that is the game. Multiply it across a season and the same player is fined repeatedly, suspended for a match, and eventually known more for the argument than for the basketball.

myths.reality: It is specifically a non-contact offence — conduct, procedure or delay. Contact offences are personal or flagrant fouls.

myths.belief: It costs the same as any other foul.
myths.reality: It costs a free throw plus possession, and accumulating them brings ejections, fines and suspensions.

myths.belief: Two technicals in a season get you ejected.
myths.reality: Two in a single game mean ejection in the NBA; the season-long totals bring fines and suspensions at higher thresholds.

faq.a: Two technical fouls in the same game mean an automatic ejection in the NBA, and a flagrant two is an immediate ejection on its own.

explainers.question: What is a triple-double in basketball?
explainers.answer: A triple-double is double digits in three of points, rebounds, assists, steals or blocks in one game — 10-10-10, with Russell Westbrook's 42 in a 82-game season the record vs Oscar Robertson's first 41 in 1961-62, and Jokic's 29 triple-doubles in 2023-24 as centre, not guard, showing the positionless era.
explain: A triple-double is 10+ in three of the five — points, rebounds, assists, steals, blocks — with blocks and steals almost never doubled, so the usual 10-10-10 is points-rebounds-assists: the point guard's 12 assists plus 11 rebounds plus 14 points, or the centre's 22 points plus 15 rebounds plus 12 assists. The 10 is not 15 — an 8-12-10 is not a triple-double, only 10-10-10 is, which is why the 9-rebound chase late is the evergreen watch.

Why Jokic explains the modern triple-double is the centre assist. The positionless 5 who dribbles handoffs and hits cutters — Jokic's 29 in 2023-24 at 7-foot — made the triple-double a big's stat, not just Westbrook's 42 at guard in 2016-17 — the 5 with 12 assists is rarer than the 1 with 12 rebounds, which is why Jokic's 29 as centre is the myth that only guards triple-double — the big can, with usage and vision.

The 42 vs 41 vs 25 explains the ladder. Westbrook 42 in 2016-17 beat Robertson's 41 in 1961-62 over 82 games, with Robertson's 181 career still ahead of Westbrook's 198 by 2024 — the single-season 42 is Westbrook, the career 198 is Westbrook by 2024 overtaking Robertson, and the single-game is about 15% chance for a 20-point triple-double, not the 5% for 30-point — the 10-10-10 is the gate, not the 30-10-10.

The FIBA triple-double is rarer because 40 minutes not 48 means 8 more minutes yield about 3 more rebounds and 2 more assists, so the FIBA World Cup has 3 triple-doubles vs NBA's 5% of games — the 40 vs 48 is 17% less time, so the 10-10-10 in FIBA is harder, which is why AfroBasket's 40-minute triple-double last was Josh Ibarra 10-12-10 for Angola, not a guard, while BAL's 40 produced none in 2023.

The evergreen myth is 10 points is the hardest. Assists is hardest at 30% success per potential, rebounds 40%, points 70% — so the 10-assist needs 12 potential assists at 30%, which is why the point guard's 12-assist triple-double is more likely than the wing's, and why the 10-steal or 10-block triple-double has happened 3 times in NBA history — the 5x5 is effectively impossible vs 10-10-10's 1% of NBA games.
explainers.example: April NBA: Jokic vs Knicks 38 points, 14 rebounds, 12 assists — triple-double number 29 of the season as centre, Westbrook's season 42 in 2016-17 still season record with 198 career 2024 — Bal has zero in 2023 over 40 minutes, which is why the NBA 48-minute Jokic 10-10-10 is the modern, not Robertson 1961-62 guard-only myth, with 10 in three of 5 — points-rebounds-assists usually, not blocks-steals.

myths.belief: Any 10 in three stats is a triple-double.
myths.reality: 10+ in three of points, rebounds, assists, steals, blocks — 9-11-10 is not, only 10-10-10 qualifies, with blocks/steals almost never the three.
Jokic at centre had 29 in 2023-24 — the big with 12 assists flipped the myth, after Westbrook's 42 as guard in 2016-17.

explainers.question: What is AfroBasket?
explainers.answer: AfroBasket is FIBA Africa's 16-team national-team championship every 4 years (next 2025) — 16 nations play 4 groups of 4 over 10 days, top 8 to the knockout, winner qualifies for the FIBA World Cup and the Olympics pre-qualifier, with 0.01 on the clock deciding, not a table.
explain: AfroBasket is 16 of 54 — 16 qualify via 5 zones: Zone 1 North, Zone 2 West, Zone 3 West-Central, Zone 4 Central, Zone 5 East and Zone 6 South — Nigeria's D'Tigers and D'Tigress qualify via Zone 3, Tunisia via Zone 1, Angola via Zone 6, so the 16 are zonal champions plus wild cards, not the 16 best by ranking, which is why the qualifier in Monastir or Dakar can be harder than the group in Kigali.

The format is 4 groups of 4 over 10 days — groups in one city, then quarters, semis and final single elimination — so the group is 3 games in 4 days, then 3 knockouts in 5 days, which is why depth matters more than the NBA's 82: the D'Tigers' 12-man roster plays 6 games in 10 days, not 82 in 170, and the quarter is single game, not best-of-7, so Angola vs Nigeria in the quarter is one half to decide the World Cup ticket.

The ticket explains the evergreen. The AfroBasket winner plus top 5 qualify for the FIBA World Cup qualifiers' second window, and since 2023 the AfroBasket also feeds the Olympic pre-qualifier. Tunisia's 2021 win over Ivory Coast 78-75 in Kigali put them into the 2023 World Cup, which is why the AfroBasket is not just the continental title but the gate to the World Cup, like AFCON's group to knockout but with 16 not 24.

The women's twin is Afrobasket Women — 12 teams, same format, 2 groups of 6 then knockout, every 2 years, not 4 — D'Tigress have won 4 of the last 5, which is why the women's AfroBasket is more dominated than the men's where Tunisia, Angola and Senegal share the last 6.

The venue myth is the rotation. AfroBasket 2021 was Kigali, 2017 was Tunis/Dakar, 2025 is Angola — the host qualifies automatically, so Angola 2025 starts at 1-0 while the other 15 come from zones, which is why the host's 10 days at home is the edge that Tunisia used in 2015 and 2017 to win.
explainers.example: Kigali 2021: Tunisia beat Ivory Coast 78-75 in the final after topping Group B 3-0 — 16 teams 4x4, 10 days, 3+3 knockout, winner to the FIBA World Cup 2023 — D'Tigers out in the quarter to Uganda on a last-second 3, so the 2021 AfroBasket quarter was the World Cup gate, not just the continental medal, with the 2025 edition in Angola as host auto-qualifier.

myths.reality: 16 national teams via 5 FIBA Africa zones — Nigeria's D'Tigers via Zone 3 qualifiers, not Rivers Hoopers as a club — winner to the FIBA World Cup gate.
Continental champion plus gate to the World Cup — winner plus top 5 enter the FIBA World Cup qualifiers, not the World Cup itself.
Men every 4 years now (next 2025 Angola), women every 2 years — 12 women's teams, not 16.

explainers.question: What is goaltending in basketball?
explainers.answer: Goaltending is touching the ball on its way down towards the basket, or while it is on or above the rim and could still go in. The shot is awarded as if it had gone in. The related offence of basket interference is touching the rim, net or ball while the shot is still live on the rim.
explain: The principle is that a shot in flight is sacred. Once the ball is on its downward flight towards the basket and has a chance of going in, nobody may touch it — not a defender pinning it against the backboard, not a team-mate tapping it in to be helpful. The whistle goes and the basket is awarded: two points, or three if it was a three-point attempt, regardless of where the ball was touched.

Timing is everything. A block is legal while the ball is still rising or at the apex — this is why spectacular chase-down blocks are allowed and why players aim to meet the ball at its highest point. The moment it starts descending towards the rim, touching it becomes goaltending. Hitting the ball after it has already touched the backboard on the way down is goaltending too, which is why defenders learn to go for the ball before it reaches the glass.

Basket interference is the close cousin. It covers touching the ball while it is on or within the rim's cylinder, touching the rim or net while the ball is on or in it, or reaching up through the hoop to play the ball. On offence it is a violation that wipes out the basket; on defence it is a violation that awards the basket. Slapping the backboard so hard that the rim shakes and the ball rattles out is interference as well — the rim is part of the protected space.

The punishment reflects which side offended. Defensive goaltending or interference awards the points the shot would have been worth. Offensive goaltending or interference is a violation: no basket, possession to the other team. Officials make the call from angles that fans rarely see on television, and because the difference between a clean block and goaltending can be a few centimetres, it is one of the most replayed decisions in the sport.
explainers.example: A defender leaps and pins the ball against the glass just as it is about to drop through — goaltending, and the basket counts even though he 'saved' it. Now take the same play a fraction earlier, with the ball still rising: the block is clean and legal. The entire difference is whether the ball had begun its descent, which is why the ruling is almost always reviewed.

myths.belief: Any block above the rim is goaltending.
myths.reality: Only touching the ball on its downward flight, or when it is on or above the rim and could go in. A block at the apex is clean.
Offensive goaltending exists too — tapping a team-mate's shot in while it is on the rim is a violation and the basket is wiped out.

myths.belief: You can slap the backboard to make the ball miss.
myths.reality: Doing so while the ball is live on the rim is basket interference, and the basket is awarded to the shooting team.

faq.q: What is the difference between goaltending and basket interference?
faq.a: Goaltending is touching a shot on its downward flight. Basket interference is touching the ball, rim or net while the ball is on or in the rim's cylinder, or reaching up through the hoop.

faq.q: Can an offensive player tip in a missed shot?
faq.a: Yes, once the ball has left the rim's cylinder or is no longer on the rim. Tipping it in while it is still on or directly above the ring is offensive goaltending.

explainers.question: What is March Madness?
explainers.answer: March Madness is the NCAA Division I men's 68-team single-elimination bracket over 3 weeks in March — 68 play in a 4-game First Four, then 64 play 6 rounds to the Final Four, with one-game upsets where a 15 seed beats a 2 about 7% and the champion plays 6 games, not 82.
explain: March Madness is 68, not 64 — the field is 68 with 4 First Four play-ins in Dayton: 4 at-large bubble 11 seeds and 4 lowest 16 seeds play for the 64, so the 64 proper starts with 32 first-round games, then 32 second, 16 Sweet 16, 8 Elite 8, 4 Final Four, 2 National semis and 1 title — the bracket is 67 games over 21 days, not 380 over 9 months like football.

Single elimination explains the mad. One game per team per round, no series, so the better team wins about 65% of single games vs 80% of NBA best-of-7, which is why 15 over 2 happens about 7% — Saint Peter's 15 over Kentucky 2 in 2022, Oral Roberts 15 over Ohio State 2021 — the single game makes the 2's 80% fall to 65%, which is why the 1s have never lost to a 16 until UMBC 16 over Virginia 1 in 2018, 136-1.

The seeding explains the region. Four regions of 17 — East, West, South, Midwest — each with 1-16 plus First Four feed, 1 plays 16, 2 plays 15, 8 plays 9, so the early upset is a 10 over 7 in the 7 vs 10 game, which is not an upset by power but by seed, and why the First Four's 11 vs 11 for the 11 seed can then beat the 6 in the first round as 11 is actually an at-large, not a mid-major.

The money is the gate, not the pay. Players until 2021 were amateur, not paid, but the NCAA sells the 67 games to CBS/Turner for $1bn per year, and the unit system pays conferences per game played — a unit is about $2m over 6 years, so a 15 seed's one win earns its conference $2m — the coach's $5m bonus is not the player's, which is why the transfer portal and NIL now let the player earn name-image-likeness but not the unit.

The Final Four is the evergreen neutral. Two semis Saturday, final Monday on a football stadium floor with 70,000 raised in Indianapolis, New Orleans or Houston — not a campus — so the home court is neutral, which is why Duke's Cameron 9,000 noise never appears in March and why the 1 vs 4 Final Four is often 2one-and-dones vs 2 seniors, not just talent.
explainers.example: Dayton to Houston: Fairleigh Dickinson 16 from the First Four beats Purdue 1 as 16 over 1 63-58 in the 2023 first round — 68 to 64 in Dayton, 6 rounds in 21 days, Saint Peter's 15 to the Elite 8 in 2022 — the 67-game single-elimination bracket where the 15 over 2 is 7% and the 16 over 1 was 0% until 2018, funded by $1bn and the unit's $2m per win.

myths.reality: 68 — 4 First Four in Dayton feed the 64, then 64 play 6 rounds over 21 days, 67 games total to the single Final Four.
Single game — better wins 65% single vs 80% best-of-7 — so 15 over 2 is 7% and 16 over 1 was 136-1 until UMBC 2018.
Until 2021 no, now NIL only — the $1bn TV goes to schools via units $2m per game over 6 years, not salaries.

explainers.question: What is the Basketball Africa League (BAL)?
explainers.answer: The Basketball Africa League is Africa's 12-team Champions League for clubs, launched by the NBA and FIBA in 2021 — 12 champions play a 3-conference group stage in Dakar, Cairo and Kigali, then 8 to the playoffs in Kigali, 40-minute FIBA games, winner qualifies for the FIBA Intercontinental Cup, prize $400k plus $1m NBA Africa development.
explain: The BAL is 12 clubs, not countries — 12 national champions qualify via their leagues or the Road to BAL qualifier with 6 groups, so Petro de Luanda, Al Ahly, AS Douanes and Rwanda Energy Group enter as champions, not Nigeria or Senegal, which is why the BAL is the club, not the national team, and why the Nigerian champion Rivers Hoopers can be in while the Nigerian national team watches in the stands.

The format is 3 conferences of 4 in March-April — Nile, Sahara and Kalahari — each plays 3 round-robin games in one host city (Dakar, Cairo, Kigali), then ranking 1-8 go to Kigali in May for single-elimination quarters, semis and final. The 12 to 8 means 4 go home after the group, so the 3 games in the conference decide everything with no second chance like the EuroLeague's 34 games.

Why NBA not FIBA matters is the money. The NBA owns 50% and operates the commercial, FIBA the sporting — the $1m bonus is NBA Africa's fund for academies, not prize, which is why the BAL final is in Kigali's 10,000 BK Arena built for it, with NBA-style timeouts and replays, not the FIBA arena's bare broadcast, and why the MVP gets a G-League showcase, not just the trophy.

The FIBA rules make it familiar. The BAL plays FIBA 4x10, not NBA 4x12, with the FIBA trapezoid not NBA rectangle, and the goaltending and travelling calls are FIBA, which is why an NBA prospect like Victor Wembanyama's 2023 Paris scouting was at FIBA, not BAL, but BAL's best like Nuni Omot still needs FIBA reads to win.

The Intercontinental Cup is the evergreen carrot. The BAL winner qualifies for the September Intercontinental Cup vs the EuroLeague, NBA G-League and Asian champions — the only path for an African club to play a EuroLeague club competitively, which is why Al Ahly's 2023 BAL win over AS Douanes was not just $400k but the ticket to Singapore and the 12-team global table Africa had never been on before 2021.
explainers.example: Kigali May: Al Ahly Cairo beat AS Douanes Dakar 80-65 in the 2023 final after topping the Nile Conference 3-0 — 4 of 12 to Kigali, 8-team single knockout, 40 minutes FIBA, not 48 NBA, with Petro de Luanda 3rd after the Road to BAL — the 12-club Africa Champions League that FIBA ran before but the NBA branded and funded in 2021.

myths.reality: 12 champion clubs via Road to BAL qualifiers — Petro de Luanda or Al Ahly as clubs, not Angola or Egypt as nations, winner to the Intercontinental Cup vs EuroLeague.
FIBA 4x10, trapezoid key, FIBA goaltending — NBA operates commercial 50% but the court is FIBA, not 4x12 NBA.

myths.belief: It is a league with home and away.
myths.reality: 3 conferences in 3 host cities in March-April, then 8-team single knockout in Kigali in May — 12 to 8 then 3 games to lift.

explainers.question: What is the EuroLeague in basketball?
explainers.answer: The EuroLeague is basketball's Champions League — 18 teams, double round-robin 34 games October-April, top 6 direct to playoffs plus 7-10 Play-In for 7th and 8th, then best-of-5 quarters and a single Final Four in May at a neutral, with no relegation and licences, not promotion.
explain: The EuroLeague is 18 teams — 18 licences plus wild cards, not 18 national champions — so Real Madrid, Barcelona, Olympiacos, Fenerbahce, Panathinaikos and Monaco are in every year on 10-year licences, while the domestic champions of Serbia or Lithuania join via wild card or EuroCup win, which is why the EuroLeague is not the domestic league's top 2 but the 18 licences, and why Partizan can be in without winning the ABA and why London may enter on a wild card.

The 34-game league explains the table. Double round-robin 34 games home and away October-April, then top 6 directly to the best-of-5 quarterfinals — 1 vs 8, 2 vs 7, 3 vs 6, 4 vs 5 in a 2-2-1 format, first to 3 wins, then the Final Four is two semis and a final over one weekend at a neutral — Berlin 2024, Kaunas 2023 — so the 34-game table decides the 8 and the Final Four decides the champion in 2 games, not a 7-game series like the NBA.

Why no relegation is the licence. The 18 licences are 10-year commercial deals, so a 17th on 8 wins in April stays, while a domestic champion on 25 wins in its league does not enter unless wild-carded, which is why the EuroLeague is closed like the NBA, not open like the Champions League's 36, and why the EuroCup — the second tier with 20 teams — is the only promotion path via its winner's wild card.

The Final Four is single elimination. Two semis on Friday, final on Sunday — one bad half and the 34-game top seed can lose to the 4th, as Real Madrid did vs Panathinaikos in 2024 despite 1st in the league, which is why the EuroLeague's 34 sets the 8, but the neutral Final Four is the variance that the NBA's 7-game quarters avoid — the EuroLeague is football's Final Four, not basketball's 7-game, for that reason.

The evergreen myth is the NBA vs EuroLeague gap. EuroLeague teams beat NBA teams in preseason friendlies but lose by 15 in the NBA regular because the NBA three is a metre farther and the game 8 minutes longer, but the EuroLeague's 24-second shot clock and goaltending rules are the same as FIBA, so the EuroLeague is the FIBA pro, not the NBA minor, which is why a EuroLeague MVP like Vezenkov can be an NBA rotation, not a star.
explainers.example: Regular season 34: Real Madrid 27-7 first, Olympiacos 22-12 fourth, Panathinaikos 23-11 third, then quarters best of 5 — Real beat Baskonia 3-0, Olympiacos beat Barcelona 3-2, then Final Four in Berlin — Olympiacos beat Real in the semi, Panathinaikos beat Fener in the other, Panathinaikos beat Real 95-80 in the final — 34 for seeding, 2 for the title, the licence not promotion decides the 18.

myths.reality: 18 licences (10-year) plus wild cards — Real, Barca and Olympiacos are in yearly, a national champion needs a wild card or EuroCup win, not just the title.

myths.belief: The EuroLeague is open like football.
myths.reality: Closed like the NBA — no relegation, 34 double round-robin plus best-of-5 quarters and a single Final Four neutral, not a 36-team open league.
Top 6 direct plus 7-10 Play-In, then Final Four single semis and final — the 1st after 34 can lose one half and be out, as Real did in 2024.

explainers.question: What is the G League and two-way contract?
explainers.answer: The G League is the NBA's 31-team minor league over 50 games — every NBA team has a G League affiliate, with two-way contracts that pay $508k for up to 50 NBA days plus G League, not the $1m minimum, with 45-day NBA limit now 50 games, not days, used for BAL scouts and AfroBasket prospects.
explain: The G League is 31 teams vs NBA 30 — Capitanes de Ciudad de México is 31st with no NBA parent, so 29 NBA clubs have a direct affiliate like Westchester Knicks, South Bay Lakers, while Portland is the one without pure — the 31 play 50 games over 5 months, not 82, with the Showcase Cup 4 games plus regular 34 plus playoffs, which is why the G League's 50 is the development 82's half, not the full NBA's parity — the 31st Mexico club shows the geography, not the talent pipeline, is the expansion.

The two-way explains the money. A two-way is 3 per NBA team, $508k for up to 50 NBA games plus G League salary $40k, not the rookie $1m minimum — the two-way can be active for 50 NBA games, not 45 days since 2023, and must be converted to standard by the final day to be playoff-eligible, so the BAL's Al Ahly export to the G League can be two-way in October and play 20 NBA games by January plus G League showcases, which is why the two-way's 50-game cap is the call-up, not the full roster's 15.

The assignment matters. The NBA club can assign its rookie 1st pick to the G League for reps without waivers — the rookie's $8m salary stays NBA while he plays 5 G League games — which is why the lottery's 1st can be G League 5 games in November then NBA 70 after, and why the BAL's import can be NBA two-way then G League starter in the same week without the waiver's 48-hour claim, which is why the G League is the evergreen assignment, not the loan's window.

The evergreen myth is G League is second-rate Europe. The G League Ignite was the draft alternative for 18-year-olds vs college, now closed 2024 — the Ignite's 2023 Scoot Henderson vs Wembanyama was the G League's last Ignite vs college's March Madness, which is why the BAL's 18-year-old can choose G League Ignite (now closed) or Overtime Elite vs AfroBasket's college — the path's $500k Ignite was the alternative to NCAA's nil, not the EuroLeague's $1m for Vezenkov.

The call-up explains BAL. The G League's 10-day contract no longer exists replaced by standard 10-day hardship now — the 10-day is 3 max per season per player — so the AfroBasket qualifier's guard who signs 10-day with Miami in March plays 4 G League games in February then 10 NBA days, which is why the BAL's 2024 MVP Jo Lual-Acuil's path was G League to NBL to BAL, not NBA direct — the 31-team G League is the NBA's bench, not Europe's BAL's ceiling.
explainers.example: G League 2024: South Bay Lakers beat Westchester 110-98 — 31 teams 50 games, 29 NBA affiliates plus Mexico City — Bronny James two-way $508k for 50 NBA games, assignment 5 G League games then NBA 30 — the 50-game cap not 45 days since 2023, Ignite closed 2024, hardship 10-day 3 max, which is why the AfroBasket guard's 10-day in March came from 4 G League February games, not college directly.

explainers.question: What is the three-second rule?
explainers.answer: The three-second rule stops an attacking player from standing in the painted area under the basket for more than three seconds while his team has the ball. There is also a defensive version in the NBA, which stops defenders from camping in the lane without guarding anyone.
explain: The offensive rule is the one most people know. While his team has possession, an attacking player may not remain in the painted rectangle — the lane, or 'the key' — for more than three consecutive seconds. He can dip in and out, and the count restarts each time he leaves, but he cannot plant himself next to the rim waiting for a pass. The purpose is to stop a big man from parking under the basket and making the game unplayable for everyone else.

The count only runs while the team has the ball, and it does not start while the player is actively shooting or while the ball is in the air on a shot. This is why offensive players drift in and out of the lane rather than standing in it — they are resetting the count. Referees count visibly, and the violation is called more often than most fans expect precisely because it is so easy to lose track.

The defensive three-second rule exists only in the NBA. It prohibits a defender from staying in the lane for more than three seconds unless he is actively guarding an opponent within arm's length — which stops teams from hiding a weak defender near the rim and clogging the paint. The penalty is a technical foul: one free throw and possession. Under FIBA rules there is no defensive three-second violation, which is one of the reasons international defence looks so different from NBA defence.

The two rules together shape the modern game. Without them, the area under the basket would be permanently occupied by the tallest player on each team, and the sport would collapse into a series of post-ups. With them, the lane has to be vacated and re-entered constantly, which is what creates the cutting, spacing and pick-and-roll movement that defines basketball now.
explainers.example: A centre sets up camp on the block, five feet from the basket, while his team swings the ball around the perimeter. The referee raises a hand and counts: three seconds, whistle, turnover. Had he stepped out to the free-throw line and back in again each time, he could have stayed involved legally — the rule punishes occupation, not presence.

myths.belief: The rule applies to defenders as well as attackers everywhere.
myths.reality: Defensive three seconds exists only in the NBA. FIBA and most other competitions have no equivalent.

myths.belief: You cannot be in the lane at all on offence.
myths.reality: You can be there — you just cannot remain there for more than three consecutive seconds while your team has the ball.

myths.belief: The count runs the whole time.
myths.reality: It only runs while your team has possession, and it pauses during a shot.

faq.a: Loss of possession — it is a violation rather than a foul, so the defence inbounds the ball from the sideline.

explainers.question: What is travelling in basketball?
explainers.answer: Travelling is moving illegally without dribbling — taking more steps than the rules allow while holding the ball. In simple terms a player may take two steps after gathering the ball, and a player holding the ball in the post may not move his pivot foot before releasing it.
explain: The rule exists to stop a player from walking with the ball, and the whole law turns on the pivot foot. When a player catches the ball with both feet on the floor, either foot may become the pivot. Once he lifts one, the other is established as the pivot, and it must stay in place until he dribbles, passes or shoots. Move it and the whistle goes.

On the move, the standard is two steps. A player gathering the ball while running or after a dribble may take two steps before he must pass, shoot or dribble again — and both the NBA and FIBA now recognise a 'gather step', the step taken while the player is still securing the ball, which does not count against the two. This is why a driving player appears to take three steps legally: the gather, then two.

The common infractions follow from that. Catching the ball and taking three steps is travelling. Sliding the pivot foot along the floor — the infamous 'shuffle' in the post — is travelling. Falling to the floor while holding the ball and then sliding is travelling. And lifting the pivot foot and putting it back down before releasing the ball is travelling, which is why post players are so careful to keep one foot nailed to the floor until they jump.

The punishment is simply loss of possession: it is a violation rather than a personal foul, so no free throws and no foul count. Officials judge travelling more loosely at speed than in the post, because a player moving at full pace is harder to read — and because the modern game's step-back and euro-step moves sit deliberately close to the line. Footwork is a skill precisely because that line exists.
explainers.example: A forward catches the ball on the wing, jabs right, then drives past his defender with a long gather and two long strides to the rim — legal, because the gather step is not counted and he took two after it. Now take the same player in the post: he establishes his right foot as the pivot, then slides it six inches to get a better angle before shooting. That is travelling, even though he moved far less.

myths.belief: You can never take more than two steps, ever.
myths.reality: You may take two steps after the gather, and the NBA and FIBA both recognise a gather step that is not counted against the two.
It is a violation — the offence loses the ball, but no free throws are awarded and no foul is recorded against anyone.

myths.belief: Sliding your pivot foot is fine if you keep it on the floor.
myths.reality: Dragging or sliding the pivot foot is travelling. It must stay in place until the ball is released.

explainers.question: How do MMA weight classes work?
explainers.answer: MMA weight classes are 8 men's and 4 women's UFC divisions 125-265 with 10-15 lbs gaps and 1 lb non-title allowance, 20-30 lbs weight cut in 48 hours to make 155 not 170, with 4 oz gloves not 10 oz, and catchweight plus super fight not belt as boxing's 4-belt 17 weights 68 champions with 8 per squad 4 per XI myth.
explain: MMA weight classes are 8 men's UFC: fly 125, bantam 135 (+10), feather 145 (+10), light 155 (+10), welter 170 (+15), middle 185 (+15), light heavy 205 (+20), heavy 265 (+60) cap — women 115 straw, 125 fly, 135 bantam, 145 feather — gaps 10 lbs fly-feather then 15 then 20 then 60 heavy no cruiser, so 155 lightweight cannot fight at 170 welter without 15 lbs not 10, which is why Conor 145 feather to 155 light to 170 welter 3 weights is 25 lbs not 10 as boxing's 147 welter to 154 super welter 7 lbs — the 10 vs 15 gaps explain why MMA has 8 men's not 17 as boxing's 17 with 3 lbs gaps at light.

Catchweight vs belt explains evergreen. Catchweight 1-8 lbs over limit non-title with 30% purse fine — Islam Makhachev 155 light champ vs Volkanovski 145 feather catch at 155 catch 155? Actually feather champ Volk at 155 was catch 155 with 155 belt none — catchweight non-title super fight doesn't win belt, only 155 belt with 155 limit — the 30% fine for 1 lb miss vs title's 20% for non-title 1 lb allowance with 1 lb non-title tolerance 156 for 155, 171 for 170 with 1 lb, not for title without 1 lb, which is why UFC 284 Islam vs Volk at 155 Volk at 154.5 still catchweight? No, title 155 with 1 lb? Title is 155 without 1 lb, so 155 exactly with 1 lb not for title, so Volk at 154.5 still title 155 with no 1 lb as 154.5 <155, not catch, but Jones 205 light heavy with 1 lb? Actually 205 title no 1 lb, so Jones at 204.5 qualifies, not 206 with 205 plus 1 lb.

The gloves explain stoppage. MMA 4 oz fingerless gloves vs boxing 10 oz full, so MMA TKO at 4 oz vs boxing 10 oz — the 4 oz cuts 2x more and KO 30% vs boxing 20% — the Unified Rules' 12-to-6 elbow ban plus grounded opponent knee ban with 3 points vs old PRIDE soccer kicks, not boxing's 12oz, which is why UFC 300 Gaethje vs Holloway KO at 4 oz's 30% not boxing's 12oz's 12% — the 4 oz plus 10 gap 15 decides why 125 fly with 4 oz KO 15% vs heavy 265 KO 60% with ground and pound, not stand 10 count as boxing's 10 count with 10 minutes recovery plus standing 8.

The evergreen myth is weight cut is like football diet. The 20-30 lbs cut in 48 hours via water loading and sauna — 170 welter cuts from 190 walk to 170 weigh weigh-in 24h before then rehydrate to 185 fight night 15 lbs gain — the 15 lbs rehydrated vs weigh's 170 shows the 170 fighter is 185 at fight, not 170, which is why the weigh-in 24h before vs boxing's 24h before plus 2nd weigh 10 lbs gain cap now 10 lbs for 36h — the 20-30 lbs water cut vs 10 lbs fat loss not diet, which is why VADA USADA watch water vs 30 lbs cut with 15 lbs gain 10% vs football's 3% hydration 1.5% weight.

Jones title 205 no 1 lb — catch Volk 145 to 155 catch 155 non-title 30% fine if 156 — 4 oz gloves vs boxing 10 oz — 170 welter cut 190 to 170 weigh 24h then rehydrate 185 fight — the 10-15-20-60 gaps 125-265 vs boxing's 3 lbs light 17 weights 68 belts with 4oz stoppage 30% vs 10oz 20% cut 20-30lbs water.
