explainers.question: What is the United Rugby Championship?
explainers.answer: The United Rugby Championship is 16 club sides from 5 nations over 18 rounds — Ireland 4, South Africa 4, Wales 4, Scotland 2, Italy 2 play 18 games not home-and-away, with cross-conference 6 vs 12, then top 8 single KO quarters and final, not the 6 Nations' national single or the Premiership's single-country 10.
explain: The URC is 16 clubs from 5 nations — Leinster, Munster, Ulster, Connacht from Ireland; Bulls, Stormers, Sharks, Lions from South Africa; Scarlets, Ospreys, Cardiff, Dragons Wales; Edinburgh, Glasgow Scotland; Treviso, Zebre Italy — 16 play 18 rounds: 12 vs own shield? Actually 4 shields Irish, Welsh, South African, Scottish-Italian — each plays each shield rival home-and-away plus 12 cross, so South African 4 vs each other 6 not 6 cross — the cross is 6 vs 10 plus 2 extra, which is why Irish shields decide Champions Cup slots with 1 per shield plus next 4 on table, not table 1-8 alone like Premiership's 10.

18 rounds explains table. Eighteen rounds over 21 weeks September-May, then 8-team knockout quarters single at higher seed, semis at higher seed, final at highest remaining — the 18 not 22 as France's Top 14 26 nor 10-team Premiership 18 with home-and-away — the URC's 18 with shields 6 internal plus 12 cross vs Top 14's 13 home-and-away with 13 reverse, which is why URC's shield winner can be 5th overall but qualify for Champions Cup via shield 1, not table 9 like Welsh 4th shield 7th overall still qualifies.

Why Stormers explains the south. Since 2021 South African 4 joined from Super Rugby — Stormers Cape Town 18k, Bulls Pretoria 51k at Loftus, Sharks Durban at Kings Park, Lions Johannesburg at Ellis — the URC final 2022 Cape Town Stormers win over Bulls 18-13 was first south final at Cape Town, not Murrayfield — the 2024 Glasgow beat Bulls at Pretoria final — the south's 18k-51k crowds vs Cardiff's 8k shows the south's pull, like IP's 132k Ahmedabad vs domestic 20k.

Champions Cup gate matters. RGC shares Champions Cup slots: Irish shield 1 plus next 3 Irish on table plus each shield winner? Actually top 8 URC qualify for European Champions Cup plus Challenge Cup for next 8 — the 8 from 16 is half, so Leinster on table 1 not just shield, plus Bulls 2, Glasgow 4, Ospreys 8 as Welsh shield — the gate is 8 of 16 vs Premiership's top 8 of 10, which is why Ospreys 8th on 50 still qualifies while Connacht 9th on 49 needs Challenge, not Champions, and why Italian Treviso with 9th Shield Italian 1 can be out of 8 but Shield Italian 1 to Challenge, not Champions as next 4 would.

The evergreen myth is URC is European only. The 16 includes 4 South African from Super Rugby since 2021 — the cross-hemisphere not just European as Top 14's 14 plus Pro D2 16 — the URC's 18 rounds single KO vs Premiership's home-and-away 18 with 4-team playoff semi double plus final single — the cross vs south shows the league's 5-nation vs nation, which is why URC's final can be in Pretoria with 51k Loftus not Twickenham's 82k as national final, with south 4 of 16.

18 rounds: shield internal plus 12 cross, not double all 15 — 7th overall can qualify as Welsh shield 1 not table 9.
Higher seed hosts — Glasgow at Pretoria 2024, Stormers at Cape Town 2022 with 51k Loftus, not neutral Twickenham 82k.

explainers.question: How does swimming at the Olympics work?

The strokes explain the 35. Freestyle 50, 100, 200, 400, 800, 1500, backstroke 100 and 200, breaststroke 100 and 200, butterfly 100 and 200, individual medley 200 and 400, plus relays 4x100 free, 4x200 free, 4x100 medley, plus the mixed 4x100 medley — the medley relay order is back, breast, fly, free so the back starts in the water, which is why the mixed medley's order can be man-woman-man-woman in any stroke but the back must start.

Rounds explain the week. The 100m has heats 64, semis 16, final 8 over two days — 64 in the morning heats, 16 in the evening semis, 8 in the next evening final — so a swimmer who makes the final swims 3 times, which is why the heats are at 80% to save the 0.01 for the final, and a 16th on 48.02 who ties for 16th swims off at 21:00 with one lane — the swim-off is the evergreen 0.01 decider that football has no equivalent for.

The polyurethane suit that covered the body added buoyancy and was banned in 2010, so the 2008-09 records in the suit still stand in some events — the 100m free suit record of 47.05 was beaten only in 2023 by 46.80, 15 years later, which is why the evergreen question is which records are suit-era and which are post-suit textile, and why the 1500m freestyle has not been broken since 2023.

The 4x100 free relay is 4x100 per nation, 8 nations in the final, with relay takeovers measured at 0.00 — the next swimmer can dive when the incoming touches, so a -0.10 takeover is a disqualification, which is why the relay's 0.00 exchange is the football offside line of swimming.

explainers.question: How does tennis seeding actually work?
explainers.answer: Tennis seeding puts the 32 best ranked into 32 of 128 at a Slam by ranking, with the 1 vs 32, 2 vs 31 on opposite halves, so the 1 and 2 can only meet in the final, the 1 and 4 only in the semi, and unseeded vs seeded is the first-round upset, not by draw luck.
explain: Tennis seeding is 32 of 128 — the top 32 in ATP or WTA enter as seeds 1-32, 32 seeds in a 128 draw means 32 seeds vs 96 unseeded in round 1, with seeds staggered so 1 plays the winner of 128 vs 33 section, not 1 vs 2 up top — the 1 vs 32 path is 1 vs 32 in the fourth round if chalk holds, not in the first, which is why the 33rd ranked is the floater who can draw the 1 in round 1 while the 32nd cannot.

The draw halves matter. Seeds 1 and 2 are opposite halves — 1 top half, 2 bottom — seeds 1-4 are quarters, so 1 can only meet 2 in the final, 1 vs 3 or 4 in the semi, 1 vs 5-8 in the quarter, which is why the US Open semi can be 1 vs 4 and the final 1 vs 2 if 1 and 2 win 6 rounds each, and why the Wimbledon grass seed can bump the ranking seed for the grass one slot, not randomly.

The unseeded floater is the evergreen upset. The 34th ranked unseeded can draw the 1 in round 1 and win 3 of 10 — Botic van de Zandschulp vs Carlos Alcaraz at US Open 2024 was unseeded vs 3 seed on day 1, not day 7 — the 33-128 floaters fill the 96 holes, so the first-round seeded upset is floater vs seed, not seed vs seed, which is why the qualifier at 180 can meet the seed at 12 in round 1 while 12 vs 13 is saved for round 3.

The seeding vs ranking gap explains protection. The seed protects for 3 rounds — 1-8 get a pass to round 3 vs 25-32, 9-16 vs 17-24 is round 3 — so a protected 6 can lose in round 1 to a floater at 45 if the floater's 3 is hot that day, but the 6's path to the quarter is 32, 17-24, 9-16, 5-8 — the ladder holds if the seed wins, but the half's 96 floaters mean the ladder's upset is daily, not weekly like football's 38.

The myth is seeding is ranking. Wimbledon until 2021 used grass formula with 75% grass points, so Federer at 3 in 2019 was seeded 2 — the ATP ranking decided 32, the grass formula decided the 1-32 order — since 2022 it mirrors ranking, but the 1-2 halves still hold, which is why the Slam draw show's ball 1 and 2 are drawn to opposite halves live, not by computer alone.
explainers.example: US Open 2024 draw: 128 draw, 32 seeds — Sinner 1 vs Mackie 110 first round, Alcaraz 3 vs Li Tu 186 first round lost, seed 1 vs seed 32 is round 4 not round 1 — 1 and 2 opposite halves, so Sinner 1 path quarter vs Medvedev 5, semi vs Draper 25, final vs Fritz 12 — the 32-seed protection that still sees 3 of 32 lose day 1 to the 33-128 floaters, and 1 vs 2 only in the final.

myths.reality: 32 of 128 by ranking, 1 and 2 opposite halves, 1 vs 32 round 4 if chalk, so 1 can only meet 2 in the final, not round 1.
They play 1 of 96 floaters 33-128 — the 34th can draw the 1 round 1 and win 3 of 10, so the floater is the upset, not seed vs seed.
32 by ranking but order can shift — Wimbledon grass formula until 2021 moved Federer 3 to 2 — now ranking mirrors but 1 and 2 halves still drawn live.

faq.q: How many seeds at a Slam?
faq.a: 32 of 128 — 1 and 2 opposite halves, 1 vs 32 round 4, 1 vs 2 only final, 96 floaters 33-128 draw seeds round 1.

faq.q: Who can draw the 1 in round 1?
faq.a: Any floater 33-128 — the 34th was van de Zandschulp vs Alcaraz 3 at US Open 2024, unseeded upset day 1.

explainers.question: How does a tennis tiebreak work?
explainers.answer: A tiebreak is first to 7 by 2 at 6-6, with serve rotation 1-2-2-2, and the Slam final-set tiebreak since 2022 is first to 10 by 2 at 6-6 — the tiebreak replaces the endless deuce game at 6-6 to decide the set in about 20 minutes, not 60.
explain: The 7-point explains the set. At 6-6, the tiebreak is first to 7 by 2 — the server serves 1 point, then the returner serves 2, 2, 2 until 7 — so the serve pattern is 1-2-2-2, change ends after 6 points, which is why the 6-6 game can end 7-6(3) where the winner took 7 points and loser 3, and why the score is 7-6(7-3), not 7-3 — the tiebreak is the 13th game of the set, not the set's second half.

The 10-point is the Slam final difference. Since 2022 every Slam plays final set at 6-6 as first to 10 by 2, not endless — Australian, French, Wimbledon and US Open all 10-point final-set super tiebreak, so the 6-6 final is 10-8, not 16-14 as Isner-Mahut 70-68 was in 2010's endless fifth before the law — the 10 by 2 saves 30 minutes and the 70-68 will never return, which is why the final-set 6-6 is now 10-point, not advantage.

Why 6-6 matters is the break. Before 6-6 the set is 6 games by 2 — 6-4, 6-3 — with no tiebreak until 6-6, so a 5-4 lead still needs a break to 6-4 or tiebreak, which is why a 6-5 service game is break point not set point, and why the tiebreak's first-to-7 is about 20 minutes, not the 45-minute 8-6 that 7-6 replaces — the tiebreak's 7 vs 10 decides 10 sets per Slam more than the 6-6 would have.

The myth is tiebreak is first to 7 always. The match tiebreak in doubles is first to 10 by 2 instead of a third set, so the doubles final can be 6-4, 6-7(3), 10-7 where the 10-7 is the match, not the set — the 10-point match vs 7-point set is the doubles bottleneck where the 3rd set is the 10-point, not a 6-4, which is why the doubles ranking includes the 10-point result as a half-set.

The Hawk-Eye myth is the let. The tiebreak has no lets on serve now since 2018 in the tiebreak, so the serve that clips and is in is played, which is why the tiebreak's 7 and 10 have more aces per point than the 6-6 game — the tiebreak's 1-2-2-2 rotation makes the 6th point the change, so the 3-3 end change is tactical, not random.
explainers.example: Wimbledon final 2023: Alcaraz vs Djokovic final set 6-6 at 4:45, tiebreak first to 7 — Alcaraz wins 7-6(7-3) at 6:05, not 14-12, with serve 1-2-2-2 rotation — Slam final-set 6-6 now 10 by 2 since 2022, so US Open semi 6-6 is 10-7 not 9-7 — the 7 by 2 normal set and 10 by 2 final set that replaced Isner-Mahut 70-68 11-hour fifth in 2010.

myths.reality: 7 by 2 at 6-6 for sets 1-4, 10 by 2 at 6-6 final set since 2022 — the match tiebreak in doubles is 10 by 2 for the deciding set.
1 point then 2-2-2 — change ends after 6, so 3-3 is the tactical switch, not every point.
Decides the set 7-6(7-3) — final set tiebreak 10-8 is the 7-6(10-8) that 2010's endless 70-68 never will be again.

faq.q: How many points in a tiebreak?
faq.a: First to 7 by 2 at 6-6 — serve 1 then 2-2-2 — final-set tiebreak since 2022 is first to 10 by 2.
7-6 set, 7-3 tiebreak — winner took 7 points, loser 3, so 7-6(7-3) is 7-3 in the breaker, 7-6 in the set.
No, doubles uses 10-point match tiebreak instead of third set — 6-4, 6-7(3), 10-7 is the match, not a set.

explainers.question: How does the ATP ranking actually work?
explainers.answer: The ATP ranking is a 52-week rolling points tally of a player's best 19 tournaments — 4 Slams plus 8 Masters 1000 mandatories plus 7 best other — with 2000 points for a Slam, 1000 for a Masters, 500 for a 500, 250 for a 250, and no points for losing first round — the ranking is the total, not the average.
explain: The 52-week roll explains movement. Points stay for 52 weeks then drop — a player who won the Australian Open for 2000 in January keeps them until next January, then defends them — so the ranking on Monday is last year's this week replaced, which is why Djokovic can be 1st without playing if his best 19 still totals more than Alcaraz's 19, and why a 3-month injury drops a player 30 places as 3 Masters worth 1000 each fall off with no replacement.

The 19 explain the ceiling. Four Slams (2000 each) plus eight Masters 1000 (1000 each) are mandatory if the player qualifies, so 12 of the 19 are fixed — the other 7 are best of the player's 500s, 250s, Challengers or United Cup — so a top 10 must play 12 plus about 7 more to keep 19, while a player ranked 80 plays 25 to find his best 7, which is why the top play 19 and the grinder plays 30 but the total is still best 19, not all.

Points per round show the ladder. Slam winner 2000, final 1200, semi 720, quarter 360, round of 16 180, round of 32 90, round of 64 45, round of 128 10 — so a quarter at a Slam is worth more than a 250 title (250), which is why a Slam quarter specialist can be top 20 without winning a title, and why a 250 title as a wild card is often the 19th that stays, not the top, for a top 10.

Why Masters are mandatory is the calendar. The 8 Masters — Indian Wells, Miami, Monte Carlo, Madrid, Rome, Canada, Cincinnati, Shanghai, Paris — are 96 or 56 draws, so 0 points for missing without medical exemption counts as a 0 in the 19, which is why a top player who skips Miami for rest takes a 0 that drags the total, not just a missed chance — the 0 is the evergreen myth that ranking is best 19, not 19 played, so a missed mandatory is a 0, not a free skip.

The live ranking vs the official explains Monday. The official ranking updates Monday after the Slam or Masters, but the live ranking during the tournament shows the points with last year's drop already removed — a player can be live 5th on Thursday and official 8th on Monday if the 2000 he defended last year was not re-earned this year, which is why the live moves during the event more than the official after.
explainers.example: Monday after the US Open: Sinner won 2000 for the US Open, kept his 2000 from last year's Australian that did not yet drop, dropped 360 from last year's Rome quarter that is now 52 weeks old, added 180 for this year's Rome round of 16 as his 19th — total 9,200, still 1st over Alcaraz on 8,500 who added a 1000 Miami win but lost a 2000 from last year's Wimbledon final that dropped that Monday — 19 best, 52-week roll, Monday update.

myths.reality: Best 19 — 4 Slams plus 8 Masters mandatories plus 7 best other — so 12 are fixed and 7 are best, not all 30 played.
Masters are mandatory — a missed mandatory without medical is a 0 in the 19, not a skip, so it drags the total like a first-round loss.
Total of best 19 over 52 weeks — the 52-week roll means points drop after 52 weeks, so a 3-month injury drops 30 places as 3 Masters fall off.

faq.q: How many points for a Slam?
faq.a: 2000 win, 1200 final, 720 semi, 360 quarter, 180 round of 16 — a Slam quarter beats a 250 title's 250.
Best 19 — 4 Slams plus 8 Masters 1000 plus 7 best other over 52 weeks, dropping after 52 weeks.

faq.q: What if a player skips a Masters?
faq.a: 0 points in the 19 if not medical — a mandatory 0, not a free skip, so the total drops.

explainers.question: How does the French Open work?
explainers.answer: The French Open (Roland Garros) is the clay Grand Slam in late May-early June at Paris — 128 singles over 15 days on crushed brick 3mm, best of 5 men, 3 women, 10-point final-set tiebreak, no roof until 2020 on Philippe-Chatrier, with 5C heat of 25°C plus wind who makes the high 1.5m bounce at 24 km/h the topspin's 8-shot rally.
explain: The French Open is 128 at Roland Garros 15 days late May — 128 men, 128 women, 20 courts 1 roof since 2020 on Chatrier 15,225, best-of-5 men, 3 women, 10-point at 6-6 final set — the crushed brick 3mm over limestone with 60cm drainage makes the 1.5m high bounce at 24 km/h with 3,000 rpm topspin sitting shoulder-high, not knee — the high bounce plus 5C 25°C plus wind 15 km/h swirl in Chatrier open makes the 8-shot rally vs US Open hard's 5, which is why Nadal's 14 titles on Philippe-Chatrier's 60m2 vs SW19's 20m grass shows the surface + wind tank.

The seeding's clay specialist myth. Roland Garros has no extra grass formula — ranking seeds 32 as other Slams — the 32 seeds split halves, 1 vs 32 round 4, 1 vs 2 final, but the clay specialist at 15 can be floater 33 vs 1 in round 1 — the 15 clay specialist at 410 points before French can meet Sinner 1 in round 1 while 32nd at 310 cannot, which is why the French first-round seeded upset is clay floater vs seed, not hard specialist, and why the new night session on Chatrier at 21:00 with roof closed makes the 25°C open not the night closed's 20°C with no wind.

The evergreen is the night session. explainers.question: What are the four Grand Slams in tennis?
explainers.answer: The four Grand Slams are the four majors — Australian Open (hard, Jan), Roland Garros (clay, May), Wimbledon (grass, July), US Open (hard, Aug) — each 128 players, best of 5 men, best of 3 women, 2000 ranking points to the winner, and the calendar Slam is winning all four in one year, last done by Rod Laver 1969 men and Steffi Graf 1988 women.
explain: The Slams are the majors because they are ITF not ATP — the ITF owns them, the ATP owns the Masters 1000, so the Slams have 128 players, 32 seeds, 64 first-round losers who still get $80k, and 2000 points vs 1000 for a Masters. The surfaces make the cycle: Melbourne hard is medium-fast, Paris clay is slow and high-bouncing, Wimbledon grass is fast and low, New York hard is fast with humidity — the same player must win on three surfaces in seven months to hold all four.

The season explains the order. Australian summer hard in January tests heat, Roland Garros clay in late May tests stamina with 5-hour rallies, Wimbledon grass two weeks later tests serve-and-volley transition on a surface that is green on Monday and brown by the semi, US hard in late August tests humidity and night matches under lights — the surface change is the evergreen reason a calendar Slam is rare, not just talent.

Best of 5 vs 3 decides the men's vs women's narrative. Men need 3 sets at Slams, women 2, so a men's 5-set can be 5 hours and a women's 2-0 can be 58 minutes — the Slams' best-of-5 for men is the only best-of-5 left after the Tour finals went best-of-3, which is why men's Slams produce comebacks from two sets down that women's cannot, and why the men's final is Sunday and the women's Saturday.

The calendar Slam vs career Slam myth matters. A calendar Slam is all four in one year — Laver 1969, Graf 1988 — a career Slam is one of each over a career — Djokovic, Nadal, Federer and Serena all have the career, not the calendar — and the Golden Slam is all four plus Olympic gold in one year, only Graf 1988, which is why the calendar remains the hardest evergreen, not the career.

The Australian heat rule shows the operation. Melbourne can suspend at 40°C heat stress, Roland Garros has a retractable roof on Philippe Chatrier since 2020, Wimbledon has a roof on Centre and No.1, US Open has two roofs — the Slams' roofs decide if the final finishes under lights at midnight, which happened at the US Open 2021 when rain pushed the women's semi to Arthur Ashe roof and the final to Sunday.
explainers.example: 2023: Djokovic won Australian hard, lost Roland Garros semi, won Wimbledon grass, lost US final — 3 of 4, not the calendar, while the women's 2023 was Sabalenka Australian, Swiatek Roland Garros, Vondrousova Wimbledon, Gauff US — four different winners, no calendar, which is why the Slams' 128-draw 2000-point four-surface cycle is the evergreen chase that 3 of 4 still feels like failure.

myths.belief: The Grand Slams are ATP events.
myths.reality: ITF majors with 128 players and 2000 points — ATP Masters are 56-96 players and 1000 points, so the Slams are the ITF's four, not the Tour's.

myths.belief: All Slams are on hard courts.
myths.reality: Australian and US are hard, Roland Garros clay, Wimbledon grass — three surfaces in seven months, which is why the calendar Slam is rare.

myths.belief: A career Slam is the same as a calendar.
myths.reality: Career is one of each over a career, calendar is all four in one year — only Laver men and Graf women have the calendar in the Open Era.

explainers.question: What is the Australian Open?
explainers.answer: The Australian Open is the hard-court Grand Slam in mid-January in Melbourne — 128 singles over 14 days in 35°C heat, best of 5 men, 3 women, with tiebreak 10 at 6-6 final set, heat rule at 4.0 wet bulb, retractable roof on 3 courts, and the Slam where the hard's 30 km/h bounce plus 40°C heat makes the 5-hour semi 40°C court.
explain: The Australian Open is 128 at Melbourne Park 14 days mid-January — 128 men, 128 women, 16 courts 3 roofs (Rod Laver 14,964, Margaret Court 7,500, John Cain 10,500), best-of-5 men, 3 women, 10-point final-set tiebreak at 6-6 as all Slams since 2022 — the hard's acrylic 30 km/h bounce 1.2m at 20°C but 35°C air adds 2 km/h bounce speed and 10% ball fluff wear per hour, which is why 35°C Melbourne mid-January plays faster than Indian Wells 30°C March, and why the heat rule closes the roof at 4.0 wet bulb globe.

The heat rule explains the delay. The AO heat stress scale 1.0-5.0 with wet bulb 32.5°C — at 4.0 the roof closes and play stops 10 minutes to cool, at 5.0 suspension — 2023 had heat rule 3 days, 2014 had 4.0 closure for 3 hours, which is why the 35°C outside is 40°C court with no wind under roof vs SW19's grass 15°C rain roof, and why the night session at 22°C after 19:00 has 70% of ticket revenue vs day's 30% because day is 35°C risk.

The seeding's bottom half matters. The AO draw's 32 seeds as all Slams, live draw halves at Crown — the bottom half's night match at Rod Laver at 19:00 is prime, top half day at 14:00 heat — the 32 seeds split halves, 1 vs 32 round 4, 1 vs 2 final, which is why Djokovic's 10 AO titles came via bottom half 7 times with night matches at 22°C, not top half day heat, and why Sinner's 2024 AO came via top half day heat 35°C not night.

The Happy Slam myth is the crowd. The AO is the Happy Slam for player facilities — $500k appearance for qualifiers plus $105k round 1 — the Happy Slam's 1m attendance over 14 days vs Wimbledon's 500k, with ground pass $60 for outer — the 1m vs 500k attendance plus 35°C vs SW19's 15°C rain explains why the AO's 14 days January is now the richest with $86m prize vs Wimbledon's $65m, which is why the AO's court is hard 30 km/h with roof, not SW19's grass 36 with queue 8mm.

The evergreen is midnight. The AO night session can run to 02:00 with best-of-5 — Murray vs Kokkinakis 04:05 2023, Hewitt vs Baghdatis 04:34 2008 — the latest finish 04:05 with roof open wind 10 km/h under lights vs US Open's 02:26 latest — the 02:00 finish is the AO's hard plus heat's late vs Wimbledon's 21:00 curfew, which is why the AO's 35°C day plus 22°C night makes the 5-hour semi 22:00 still 30°C with roof closed.

myths.reality: Outdoor hard 30 km/h 1.2m bounce but 35°C air adds 2 km/h vs SW19 15°C — 3 roofs close at 4.0 heat, night session 22°C is the prime, not day heat.
Wet bulb 4.0 closes roof — 2023 heat rule 3 days at 35°C outside 40°C court — midnight finishes 04:05 under lights, latest of Slams.
1m attendance over 14 days vs Wimbledon 500k — $86m prize vs $65m, hard 30 vs grass 36 with ground pass $60 not £27 queue.

explainers.question: What are the Davis Cup and Billie Jean King Cup?
explainers.answer: The Davis Cup (men) and Billie Jean King Cup (women) are the national-team World Cups of tennis — 16 teams in the Finals each November, with ties of 2 singles and 1 doubles over 1 day, played home-or-away in the qualifiers with 128+ nations in the pyramid, not the 128-player Slam draw.
explain: The Davis Cup is nations, not players — Canada vs Italy is 3 matches: 2 singles and 1 doubles over one day, best of 3 ties, with singles 4 of 96 and doubles 1 of 48 plus doubles team, so the World No 1 can lose if his No 2 loses both singles, which is why Sinner can be 1 but Italy without Sinner can still lose the qualifier tie at home — the 2+1 makes the 2nd singles the tie, not the star.

The pyramid widens it. Qualifiers February are 24 ties home-or-away knockout, winners to September Finals group of 16 in 4 groups of 4 over 6 days, then 8-team knockout November in Malaga or Seville — the Billie Jean King Cup mirrored with 12 not 16 — so the 128 nations play home ties in zone groups September-February before the 16-team Finals, which is why tennis has a February home Davis Cup week with 5,000 crowds not on TV but the November Finals on centre court with Hawkeye.

The surface choice decides. The home nation chooses surface — Spain chooses clay in Cordoba, USA chooses hard in New York, Great Britain indoor hard in Glasgow — so the tie's 2+1 can be loaded for the host's clay specialist over the visitor's hard hitter, which is why the Davis Cup upset is surface, not ranking — Argentina on clay beat USA on clay in 2008 with Nalbandian beating Roddick on clay, not hard.

The evergreen myth is Davis Cup is doubles only. It is 2 singles plus doubles — the 3rd singles matters if split 1-1 after day 1 would have been, but since 2019 the format is 2 singles plus doubles over one day, so a 2-0 lead wins before doubles, which is why the ticket says 2 singles first then doubles, not doubles first, and why the fan buys 1 day not 3.

The ATP and WTA do not rank Davis Cup points — zero since 2016, so the tie is pride plus $15m prize pool not ranking, which is why top 10 can skip the February qualifier and still be 1 seed at March Masters — the ranking and the Cup are separate, like AFCON's group vs league points.
explainers.example: February qualifier: Italy vs Netherlands in Bologna indoor hard — Italy without Sinner lose singles 1 and doubles but win singles 2, 1-2 loses the tie — November Finals in Malaga Group A Italy beat Chile 2-1 then quarters vs Netherlands 2-0, same 2+1 — the 3-match tie with 16-team Finals November after 24 February home-or-away qualifiers with 128 nations descending to 16, surface chosen by host.

myths.reality: 2 singles plus 1 doubles over 1 day — 2-0 ends before doubles, so the 2nd singles decides more ties than the doubles.
February 24 qualifiers home-or-away, September 4x4 Finals group, November 8-team knockout — the 6 days not the 12-month league.
Zero since 2016 — $15m prize not ATP points, so the No 1 can skip February and still be 1 in March.

faq.a: Men's tennis World Cup — 16 teams in Finals November, ties 2 singles plus 1 doubles over 1 day, 24 February home-or-away qualifiers feeding the 16.

faq.q: What is the Billie Jean King Cup?
faq.a: Women's equivalent — 12 Finals in November, same 2+1 tie format over 1 day, named after the pioneer.

faq.q: Does Davis Cup give ranking points?
faq.a: No since 2016 — prize and pride, not ATP points, so top 10 can skip qualifiers.

explainers.question: What is Wimbledon and how does it work?
explainers.answer: Wimbledon is the grass Grand Slam in early July at SW19 London — 128 singles, best of 5 for men, 3 for women, over 14 days with white clothing, no Hawkeye until 2007, no tiebreak until 2019, queue instead of ballot, and the Ballon d'Or of tennis where the serve wins 60% on grass vs 42% on clay.
explain: Wimbledon is 128 over 14 days — 128 men's singles, 128 women's, best of 5 for men (first to 3 sets, 6 games per set with tiebreak 7 at 6-6, final set 10 at 6-6 since 2022), best of 3 for women, doubles same, with the middle Sunday now day 7 since 2022 after the rain-less roof era — the queue outside SW19 coaches for 1,500 ground passes at £27 vs debenture £80k for Centre 1,500 seats, which is why the ballot's 150k applicants compete for 41,500 capacity over 14 days, not just screen.

Grass explains success. The 100% rye at 8mm cut daily to 8mm gives low bounce 1.0m at 36 km/h after, serve wins 60% on grass vs 54% hard 42% clay, so the ace's 10 per match vs 5 on clay decides — the 36 km/h low bounce on rye at SW19 at 15°C with roof closed adds 2 mph vs open 20°C wind, which is why the roof's 10 minute close with 30 km/h wind off saves the final's 6pm light vs Roland Garros's clay 22°C open's 24 km/h high bounce.

The clothing is the myth. All white with 10mm colour trim since 1887 — the white's 10mm is measured, cream fails the test — the 2023 easing allows dark undershorts for women, not coloured dress — the 10mm white is the evergreen that costs the player $500 for a non-white shoe's red sole, which is why Kyrgios' red Air Jordan was banned in 2022 while his white one passed, and why the queue's white dress code still fines the junior's 11mm trim.

The tiebreak's 2019 ended endless. Wimbledon had no tiebreak final set before 2019, so Isner-Mahut 70-68 11 hours over 3 days 2010's final set 70-68 at 70 games — since 2019 at 12-12 final-set tiebreak, since 2022 at 6-6 final-set 10 by 2 — the 10-point at 6-6 10-7 replaces the 70-68, which is why the 2023 Alcaraz-Djokovic 1-6,7-6(6),6-1,3-6,6-4 had no 10-point final but 6-4, not 10-7, because it ended before 6-6, not after as 2019 would have demanded.

The queue vs ballot explains tickets. The ballot is September lottery for 50% of tickets, the queue is overnight camp with numbered queue card for ground pass £27 day 1 for Court 3, debenture is 5-year £80k for Centre's 1,500 seats sold via corporate, which is why the queue's 10:00 line at Wimbledon Park 7am with 8-hour wait still beats StubHub's £5,000 Centre final vs debenture holder's resale, and why SW19 has 18 courts not 1.
explainers.example: Wimbledon 2023 Centre: SW19 14 days July — 128 men best-of-5, women best-of-3 — grass 1.0m 36 km/h vs clay 1.5m 24 — Alcaraz vs Djokovic final 1-6,7-6(6),6-1,3-6,6-4 over 4:42, final set 6-4 not 10-7 as 6-4 before 6-6 — All white 10mm, queue 1,500 ground £27 vs debenture £80k, Isner-Mahut 70-68 before 2019's 12-12 tiebreak.

explainers.question: Why do tennis players challenge with Hawk-Eye?
explainers.answer: Hawk-Eye in tennis is 10 cameras tracking the ball at 340 fps to the millimetre, and the challenge lets a player ask the system to overrule the line judge — 3 challenges per set, 1 extra at tiebreak, correct keeps the challenge, wrong loses it — with an average 25% overturn rate because the human eye misses by 3-5mm at 130 mph.
explain: Hawk-Eye is 10 high-speed cameras around the court triangulating the ball's centre at 340 frames per second to about 2.6mm accuracy, then rendering the bounce as a graphic in 10 seconds — the line judge calls in 0.3 seconds at 130 mph, Hawk-Eye confirms in 10 seconds at 2.6mm, which is why the challenge exists — the eye cannot see 3mm at 130 mph, the system can to 2.6mm, and the biggest error is on the line where the eye's parallax is worst.

The challenge explains the number. Three per set, plus one at tiebreak, with correct challenges retained — so a player who challenges three times and is right three times still has three, while three wrongs leave zero and a wrong at 30-40 can cost the game — the 3 is the bottleneck that stops every point being challenged, which would add 10 seconds per point and make a 3-hour match 4 hours.

On-court vs live explains the show. The stadium screen shows the bounce in slow motion with the mark — in for a 1mm, out for a 2mm — and the crowd roars at the graphic, which is why the challenge is the most televised 10 seconds in tennis — the player's challenge is the fan's replay, and the umpire's call stands if Hawk-Eye is unavailable, which is why some Challengers with no Hawk-Eye still use the human call only.

The other Hawk-Eye is offside. The same Hawk-Eye company does football's goal-line 500Hz watch, but tennis's 340 fps is ball vs line, not ball vs defender — the tennis bounce is the decision, the football goal-line is the sensor, and the tennis challenge is player-initiated while football's GLT is automatic, which is why tennis players control the challenge and football players do not.

The evergreen myth is the mark. On clay the ball leaves a mark, so Roland Garros did not use Hawk-Eye until 2024 on small courts because the mark was the judge and the umpire would walk to check it — the 3mm mark on clay is visible, on hard it is not, so hard and grass use Hawk-Eye and the player challenges, clay used the mark and the umpire, which is why the 2024 Roland Garros Hawk-Eye on hard courts was the last clay holdout.
explainers.example: US Open: Swiatek serves at 120 mph on break point, the line judge calls out, Swiatek challenges with 2 left, Hawk-Eye shows the ball's centre 2mm inside the line at 340 fps — in, correct, challenge stays at 2, point replayed as let if the call was out before the rally, or awarded if the out call was late — the 10-second 2.6mm graphic that overturns the 0.3-second human at 130 mph, 3 per set, 25% overturn.

myths.reality: About 2.6mm accuracy at 340 fps — the 3mm mark on clay is the human vs system margin, which is why the overturn is 25% not 50%.
3 per set plus 1 at tiebreak, correct keeps, wrong loses — three wrongs and no challenges left for the tiebreak, so the 3 is the bottleneck.
The player's challenge triggers the 10-second graphic that overrules the line judge — the player, not TV, initiates the overrule.

faq.a: 3 per set plus 1 at tiebreak — correct keeps, wrong loses, so three wrongs leave zero for the rest of the set.
About 2.6mm at 340 frames per second — the human eye misses by 3-5mm at 130 mph, so 25% are overturned.

explainers.question: Why is tennis different on clay, grass and hard?
explainers.answer: Clay, grass and hard are three sports on one court — clay bounces high and slow at 24 km/h after bounce, hard medium at 30, grass low and fast at 36, so the rally is 8 shots on clay, 5 on hard, 3 on grass, and the Ballon d'Or of tennis is the player who wins on all three.
explain: Clay slows and bounces high — crushed brick 3mm over stone, bounce 1.5m high at 24 km/h after, rally 8 shots, slide 1m, ball leaves a mark, Hawkeye not needed until 2024 — the clay season is April-June with Monte Carlo, Madrid, Rome and Roland Garros's 42 days of slide, which is why Nadal's 14 Roland Garros on clay is the surface specialist — the high bounce lets the topspin's 3,000 rpm sit up at shoulder height, not knee, so the clay grinder wins with spin, not serve.

Hard sits in the middle — acrylic 10mm over concrete, bounce 1.2m at 30 km/h, rally 5 shots, no slide, the US Open and Australian Open on hard with identical speed but different balls — the hard's medium forces the all-court player, which is why Djokovic's 24 Slams split 10 on hard, 3 on clay, 7 on grass — the hard's 5-ball rally is serve plus one, not serve plus seven as on clay.

Grass is skids and stays low — rye 8mm cut to 8mm morning, bounce 1.0m at 36 km/h after, rally 3 shots, slip not slide, the ball stays knee-high at 130 mph, which is why Federer's 8 Wimbledons on grass were serve-and-volley and slice, not topspin, and why Djokovic's 7 on grass still trailed Federer's 8 — the low 36 km/h bounce makes return 0.2 seconds faster than clay's 24, so the serve's 60% first-serve points won on grass vs 42% on clay.

The evergreen is transition cost. The clay-to-grass switches in 14 days — Roland Garros final Sunday, Wimbledon first Monday 14 days later — the big step from slide to slip in 14 days favours the all-courter, which is why the Channel Slam — French plus Wimbledon same year — has happened 11 times men: Borg 3, Nadal 2, Federer 1, Djokovic 1 — the 14-day surface switch is the bottleneck that beat Lendl who never made it.

The shoe and ball explain the myth. Clay shoes have herringbone for slide, grass has nubs for grip, hard flat — the ball is heavy extra duty for clay, regular for hard, extra for grass with fuzz, so the same 130 mph serve is 10 km/h slower on clay after bounce than on grass, measured by Hawk-Eye's 340 fps, which is why Hawkeye is 2.6mm on hard/grass but the mark is eye on clay — the surface's friction decides the ranking that month, not just the player.
explainers.example: Season: Roland Garros clay bounce 1.5m 24 km/h rally 8, Wimbledon grass 1.0m 36 km/h rally 3, US Open hard 1.2m 30 km/h rally 5 — same 15-30-40 scoring, three sports in one year, 14 days clay-to-grass — Nadal 14 clay, Federer 8 grass, Djokovic 10 hard — the 8 vs 5 vs 3 shot rally that makes the French winner rarely the Wimbledon winner unless the 14-day switch is mastered.

myths.reality: Clay high-slow 8 shots 24 km/h, hard medium 5 at 30, grass low-fast 3 at 36 — three sports, not one, with slide vs slip vs none.
Fastest — 36 km/h after bounce low at knee vs clay's slow high 24 at shoulder — so grass favours serve, clay topspin.

myths.reality: Channel Slam French+Wimbledon same year 11 times men — Borg 3, Nadal 2 — the 14-day switch is the evergreen bottleneck.
